t: Rendering strategies: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming
one: Where and when HTML is produced: in the browser, on the server per request, at build time, or at build time with periodic refresh.
an: CSR is a flat-pack kit the customer assembles at home. SSR is a chef cooking each order fresh. SSG is pre-made sandwiches on the shelf. ISR restocks the shelf every so often.
how: CSR: empty HTML + JS bundle; the browser fetches data and renders. Simple hosting, slow first paint, weak SEO without help.
SSR: server renders HTML per request with fresh data, then the client hydrates. Good first paint and SEO; needs a server; TTFB depends on data speed.

SSG: HTML generated at build time, served from CDN. Fastest; data is as old as the last build. ISR / revalidation: regenerate pages in the background on a schedule or on demand (Next.js: revalidate, revalidateTag(tag, profile)).
Streaming SSR: send the page shell immediately and stream slower sections as they resolve (React Suspense).

Partial prerendering: a static shell from the CDN with dynamic “holes” streamed per request. In Next.js 16 you opt in with cacheComponents: true and mark cached work with 'use cache'; the old experimental.ppr flag is removed.
why: This is the central frontend architecture decision. Seniors pick per route: marketing pages static, dashboards client or server, product pages ISR.
trade: SSR shifts cost to servers and couples page speed to backend speed. CSR shifts it to users' devices. Caching strategy follows the choice.

myth.r: SSR improves first paint, but hydration can delay interactivity, and slow data makes TTFB slow. It depends on data and device.

q.s: A product catalogue with 50k pages; prices change a few times a day; SEO matters. Strategy?
o: Pure CSR
SSG/ISR with on-demand revalidation when a product changes
SSR every request with no cache
Rebuild all 50k pages hourly
q.e: Static-speed pages, updated only when data actually changes.

more: TTFB vs FCP vs LCP trade-offs per strategy
SEO and social previews for CSR apps
lab: Build one Next.js page four ways: client fetch, server-rendered per request, static at build, and revalidated every 60 seconds. Compare TTFB, LCP and the HTML source (View Source) of each.
Throttle to Slow 4G + 4× CPU and repeat.

plain:
The HTML a user sees can be produced in different places and at different times. CSR: in the browser, after JavaScript loads. SSR: on the server, for every request. SSG: once, at build time. ISR: at build time, then refreshed in the background every so often or when data changes.

Each choice trades speed, freshness, server cost and SEO differently. Good apps choose per page.
bridge: A Vite + React app is CSR. Next.js lets you pick per route: a marketing page can be static, a dashboard client-rendered, a product page regenerated when the product changes.

walk.title: Choosing a strategy for each page of a shop
steps: Home and About: same for everyone, rarely change → static (SSG). Served instantly from the CDN.
Product pages: 50,000 of them, important for SEO, prices change a few times a day → ISR with on-demand revalidation when a product is edited.
Search results: depend on the query, must be fresh → SSR (or CSR for the results list).
Account dashboard: private, behind login, no SEO → CSR or SSR with no caching.
One app, four strategies, each chosen for that page's needs.

terms: Client-side rendering: the browser builds the page with JS.
Static site generation at build time.
Incremental static regeneration: static pages refreshed later.
Time to first byte from the server.
insights: The choice is per route, not per app. Most real apps mix three or four strategies.
A CDN cache changes what users actually get: an SSR page behind a 60-second shared cache behaves like ISR. Decide rendering and caching together.
The expensive bug here is not slowness but leakage: one user's personalised HTML stored in a shared cache and shown to other users.

prod.summary: In production you choose rendering per route and then design the cache around it. Seniors watch three things: how fresh the data must be, what TTFB/LCP the route gets at p75, and how a content change reaches the cache (time-based or on-demand invalidation).
checklist: Each route has a written reason for its strategy (static, ISR, SSR, CSR) and a freshness target, e.g. “price visible within 1 minute of edit”.
On-demand invalidation is wired to the write path: the admin save calls revalidateTag/revalidatePath, not only a timer.
Personalised or cookie-based data never ends up in a shared cache (check Cache-Control on SSR responses: private or no-store for user pages).
Slow data is wrapped in <Suspense> so the shell streams; one slow API must not hold the whole TTFB.
Field data (CrUX or RUM), not only Lighthouse, shows LCP at p75 per route type.
generateStaticParams pre-builds only the popular pages; the long tail renders on first request (dynamicParams is true by default).
View Source on a CSR route: if the HTML body is empty, social previews and some crawlers see nothing.
numbers: web.dev thresholds at the 75th percentile: LCP “good” is 2.5 s or less; TTFB “good” is 0.8 s or less.
Next.js 16: revalidateTag needs a second argument (a cacheLife profile such as 'max'); the one-argument form is deprecated.
Next.js 16 removed the “Size” and “First Load JS” columns from next build output; measure real routes with Lighthouse or RUM instead.
failures: Product price changed in the admin, but the page shows the old price for an hour.
The page only uses time-based revalidate = 3600. Tag the data fetch and call revalidateTag('product-42', 'max') (or updateTag inside a Server Action for read-your-writes) when the product is saved.
User A sees user B's name in the header after a deploy.
A personalised SSR page was cached by the CDN because it was served with a public Cache-Control. Mark user-specific responses private, no-store, and keep personal parts out of static/ISR routes.
TTFB on the SSR dashboard jumps from 300 ms to 2.5 s.
One slow backend call is awaited before any HTML is sent. Move it into a component inside <Suspense> so the shell streams first, or fetch in parallel instead of in sequence.
Build takes 40 minutes after adding 50k product pages.
generateStaticParams returns every product. Return only the top N, let the rest render on first request and cache them (ISR).
Link previews in Slack/Telegram show a blank card.
The route is CSR, so the HTML has no <title> or Open Graph tags. Render metadata on the server (Next.js generateMetadata).

code.note: The tag links the cached fetch to the write. Time-based revalidate is only a fallback; the edit itself triggers the refresh.

qs.s: A news site renders article pages with SSR on every request. Traffic spikes 20× after a big story and the origin servers fall over, although the article text is identical for all readers. Best fix?
o: Add more SSR servers and an autoscaler
Switch the article route to CSR so browsers do the work
Make the article static/ISR and invalidate it when the editor saves
Cache the database query in Redis and keep SSR
qs.e: Identical content for all users is the ideal case for static output on a CDN; a spike then hits the CDN, not your servers. Redis still leaves rendering per request on the origin, and CSR hurts SEO and first paint for a news site.

qs.s: Your SSR route awaits three API calls one after another: user (100 ms), recommendations (900 ms), cart (150 ms). TTFB is about 1.2 s. Which change gives the biggest TTFB win while keeping the same data on the page?
o: Stream: send the shell first and put recommendations inside <Suspense>; start the other calls in parallel
Cache the whole SSR HTML for every user for 60 s
Move all three calls to the client with useEffect
Increase the server's CPU
qs.e: TTFB is waiting for data, not CPU. Parallel calls cut the wait to the slowest call, and streaming lets the shell go out before the slow 900 ms call. A shared 60 s cache would mix up per-user carts.

qs.s: An ISR page has revalidate = 60. Nobody visits it for 3 hours, then one user opens it. What does that first user see?
o: A 3-hour-old error page
The fresh page, because ISR regenerates before responding
A blank page while it rebuilds
The old cached page; a background regeneration starts, and later visitors get the new one
qs.e: ISR is stale-while-revalidate: the timer only marks the page stale. The first request after that still gets the cached version and triggers regeneration. If “first viewer must see fresh data” matters, use on-demand revalidation on write.

qs.s: Next.js 16 with cacheComponents: true. next build fails on this page with “Next.js encountered uncached or runtime data during prerendering … cookies() … accessed outside of <Suspense>”. getProducts() uses 'use cache'. What is the right fix?

code.title: app/page.tsx

o: Add export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' to the page
Turn off cacheComponents, because cookies cannot be used with it
Move the cookie read into a small <UserMenu /> component wrapped in <Suspense>; the product grid stays in the prerendered static shell
Wrap the await cookies() call in try/catch
qs.e: With Cache Components, anything that needs the request (cookies, headers, uncached fetches) must sit inside a <Suspense> boundary, so the rest of the page can be prerendered as a static shell and the dynamic part streams in. force-dynamic belongs to the old model: with cacheComponents enabled, next build rejects it (“Route segment config "dynamic" is not compatible with nextConfig.cacheComponents”), and even where it works it makes the whole page dynamic and throws away the fast static shell.

qs.s: Your CDN serves a product page. Read the response headers. A user requests the page when the cached copy is 330 seconds old. What happens?

code.title: curl -sI https://shop.example.com/p/42
code.src:
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
cache-control: public, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60
age: 330
x-cache: HIT

o: The CDN returns the stale copy immediately and refreshes it from the origin in the background
The CDN waits for the origin to render a fresh page before answering
The CDN returns 504 because the copy is older than s-maxage
The browser serves the page from its own cache for another 60 seconds
qs.e: Fresh for 300 s, then a 60 s stale window (300–360 s). At 330 s the CDN may serve stale and revalidate in the background, so this user is fast but sees slightly old data. After 360 s the CDN must wait for the origin. s-maxage applies to shared caches only, so the browser cache is not involved here.

qs.s: You converted a product page to streaming SSR: the shell is sent at once and the product details stream inside <Suspense>. TTFB dropped from 900 ms to 120 ms, but p75 LCP got worse. What is the most likely reason?
o: Streaming disables HTTP compression
The CDN cannot cache streamed responses
Hydration now starts later
The LCP element (the main product image) is inside the Suspense boundary, so it arrives only when the slow data resolves, after the fallback skeleton was painted
qs.e: Streaming helps TTFB and FCP, but LCP measures the largest content element. If that element streams late, LCP waits for the slow data anyway, plus the skeleton swap. Keep the LCP content (title, hero image) in the shell or in a fast boundary, and stream secondary parts like reviews and recommendations.

qs.s: You moved SSR from one region (next to the database in Frankfurt) to edge functions around the world. Each page makes 3 sequential DB queries. Users in Tashkent now see a higher TTFB. Why?
o: Edge functions have a slower CPU
The renderer moved closer to the user but away from the data: every query now crosses a long network path, and 3 sequential queries pay that round trip 3 times
Edge functions cannot stream HTML
The CDN cache is disabled for edge functions
qs.e: Latency to the data usually matters more than latency to the user, because a page makes several data calls but only one user round trip. Render close to the data (regional), or use the edge only for cached or data-free work. A slower CPU is not the main cost; network round trips are.

interview.q: How would you choose rendering strategies for a large e-commerce site in Next.js 16?
answer: Decide per route by three questions: is the content the same for everyone, how fresh must it be, and does SEO matter.
Marketing and category pages: static, with on-demand revalidation (revalidateTag) wired to the CMS or admin save.
Product pages: static shell with cached product data ('use cache' + cacheTag), with price/stock or the user's cart streamed in <Suspense> (Partial Prerendering).
Account and checkout: dynamic per request, Cache-Control: private, no-store, never in a shared cache.
Search: SSR for the first results page (SEO for popular queries), client fetching for filters after that.
Measure with field data (p75 LCP, INP, TTFB per route type) and check the build output to confirm which routes are static.
followups: A product has 50,000 variants. Do you prebuild them all?
How do you make sure a price change is visible within one minute?
What goes wrong if a personalised component ends up inside the cached shell?

interview.q: p75 LCP on the product page went from 2.1 s to 3.8 s after a release. Walk me through how you debug it.
answer: Check if it is real and where: RUM split by route, device type and country; compare with CrUX. Find the release that changed it.
Use the LCP attribution (web-vitals attribution build): which element is LCP, and how the time splits into TTFB, resource load delay, resource load time and render delay.

High TTFB → server or data problem (slow query, cache miss, region). High load delay → the image is discovered late (lazy-loaded, CSS background, injected by JS). High render delay → render-blocking CSS/JS or the element waits for hydration or a Suspense boundary.
Reproduce with a throttled trace (slow 4G, 4× CPU) and diff the network waterfall against the previous release.
Fix the specific phase, add a guard (Lighthouse CI or a RUM alert on p75 per route) so it does not come back.
followups: Lab LCP is fine but field LCP is bad. What could explain it?
How does a cookie banner become the LCP element, and is that a problem?

interview.q: Explain Partial Prerendering / Cache Components in Next.js 16. How does it change how you think about caching compared with the older App Router?
answer: Old model: a whole route was either static or dynamic, and one cookies() call made the whole route dynamic. fetch caching was implicit and surprised people.
New model: everything is dynamic by default; you opt in to caching explicitly with 'use cache', cacheLife and cacheTag on functions or components.
At build time Next.js prerenders a static shell from everything that is cached or does not need the request; request-time parts must be inside <Suspense> and stream in.
Invalidation: updateTag in a Server Action for read-your-own-writes, revalidateTag(tag, profile) for stale-while-revalidate elsewhere.
Trade-off: more explicit code and new build errors, but one route can now be mostly static and partly personal, which used to need client fetching.
followups: What happens if you read cookies() inside a 'use cache' function?
How do you test that a route still produces a static shell?

videos.why: Ten rendering patterns compared in seven minutes.
CSR, SSR, SSG and ISR explained one at a time.

one: Hydration is the client re-running components over server-rendered HTML to attach event handlers and state. Islands hydrate only the interactive parts.
an: A printed photo of a dashboard arrives first. Hydration is wiring every button behind the photo so it actually works. Islands wire only the few buttons that need it.
how: After SSR, the browser downloads the JS for every client component on the page and renders them again in memory. React then attaches event handlers to the existing DOM instead of creating new nodes. Until this finishes, buttons look ready but do nothing.

Hydration mismatch: the client's first render differs from the server HTML (dates, Math.random, window checks, locale formatting, invalid HTML nesting). React 19 reports a recoverable “Hydration failed” error, throws away the server HTML up to the nearest <Suspense> boundary (the whole root if there is none) and renders that part on the client. Users see a flicker and you pay for rendering twice.

Selective hydration (React 18+): content inside <Suspense> hydrates in separate chunks, and if the user clicks a part that is not hydrated yet, React hydrates that part first and then replays the click.
Islands (Astro, Fresh) and React Server Components reduce what must hydrate at all. Islands can also delay hydration until a component is visible or the browser is idle.
why: Large hydration cost is a main cause of poor INP on SSR sites. Mismatch bugs are common in real apps.
trade: Fewer hydrated parts means less JS but more care about where the client/server boundary sits.

myth.r: Classic SSR ships and executes the same JS as CSR, plus the HTML. RSC and islands are what reduce JS.

q.s: A component renders new Date().toLocaleTimeString() and you get hydration warnings. Why?
o: CSS bug
Server and client produce different text (time passed, different timezone/locale)
Missing key prop
CORS
q.e: Render time-dependent values only on the client (after mount) or pass a fixed value from the server.

lab: Create a hydration mismatch on purpose (render Date.now()), read the error, then fix it with a client-only effect.
Build the same small page in Astro with one interactive island and compare the JS shipped.

plain:
With server rendering, the browser first receives ready HTML, so the page appears quickly. But buttons do not work yet. Hydration is the step where React loads in the browser, runs your components again, and attaches event handlers to that existing HTML.

Until hydration finishes, the page looks ready but does not respond. If the browser renders something different from the server, you get a hydration mismatch error.
bridge: In React 19 the error reads “Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client. As a result this tree will be regenerated on the client.” (React 18 said “Text content does not match server-rendered HTML”). A common cause is rendering new Date() or window.innerWidth during render.

walk.title: A hydration mismatch and its fix
steps: A component renders Last updated: {new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}.
The server renders “10:00:01” (server time zone, UTC). The HTML is sent.
The browser hydrates a second later in Tashkent (UTC+5) and renders “15:00:02”.

React finds different text and reports a “Hydration failed” error. It discards the server HTML up to the nearest <Suspense> boundary (or the whole page if there is none) and renders it again on the client.

Fix: render a stable value on the server (a fixed time zone) and switch to local time in useEffect after hydration, or pass the timestamp as a prop and format it with an explicit timeZone on both sides.

terms: Server and client rendered different output.
Only the interactive parts of a page hydrate.
When the page actually responds to input.
insights: A page can look finished and still be dead. Test the first seconds on a slow phone: tap a button right after the page appears.
Every mismatch costs twice: the server render is thrown away and the client renders the same part again, often with a visible flicker.
Hydration cost grows with the number of client components on the page, not with the size of the HTML. Count client components on your heaviest route.

prod.summary: In production, hydration shows up as two problems: slow interactivity on mid-range phones (large JS to download and run before buttons work) and mismatch errors that make React throw away server HTML and re-render on the client. Seniors keep the hydrated part small and treat every mismatch as a bug, not a warning to silence.
checklist: Zero hydration errors in the browser console and in error tracking (Sentry etc.) on the main routes.
No browser-only values in render: window, localStorage, Date.now(), Math.random(), navigator.language. Use useEffect, useId or pass the value from the server.
Dates and numbers are formatted with an explicit locale and timeZone, so server and browser produce the same text.
Valid HTML nesting: no <div> inside <p>, no <a> inside <a>; the browser parser rewrites these and React then sees different DOM.
suppressHydrationWarning is used only for a single unavoidable text (like a timestamp), never on a whole subtree.
Heavy, below-the-fold widgets are lazy or behind <Suspense> so React can hydrate the important parts first (selective hydration).
INP and total JS execution are measured on a real mid-range Android device, not only a MacBook.
numbers: INP (Interaction to Next Paint) is “good” at 200 ms or less and “poor” above 500 ms at the 75th percentile (web.dev).
A “long task” is any main-thread task over 50 ms; hydration of a large tree is often one or several long tasks.
suppressHydrationWarning works only one level deep: on the element's own attributes and text, not its children.
failures: Sentry shows “Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client” on every page load in one country.
Dates are formatted with the default locale/time zone, which differs between server (UTC) and browser. Format with a fixed timeZone on both sides, or render the local time only after mount.
Mismatch errors appear only for some users and you cannot reproduce them.

A browser extension (translator, password manager, Grammarly) changes the DOM before React hydrates. React 19 skips unexpected tags in <head>/<body>, but changes inside your own tree still mismatch. Confirm with a clean profile; do not hide real bugs behind this excuse.
Buttons do nothing for 2–3 seconds after the page appears on cheap Android phones.
Hydration of one big tree blocks the main thread. Move static parts to Server Components, lazy-load heavy widgets, and split with <Suspense> so hydration happens in smaller chunks.
Layout flickers: the logged-in header flashes to the logged-out version after load.
The server rendered “logged out” (no cookie read) while the client read localStorage. Read the session on the server (cookie) so both renders agree.

code.title: Rendering a local time without a hydration mismatch
code.note: The initial state is deterministic, so hydration matches. The browser-specific value arrives one render later, inside useEffect.

qs.s: A component renders <p><ProductCard /></p>, and ProductCard returns a <div>. In dev you get a hydration error, but the code looks deterministic. Why?
o: React does not allow components inside paragraphs
The CSS for p differs between server and client
ProductCard needs a key
A div inside p is invalid HTML; the browser's parser closes the p early, so the real DOM differs from what React expects
qs.e: Invalid nesting is a classic non-obvious mismatch. The server string is fine, but the HTML parser “fixes” it into a different tree before React hydrates. Use a div wrapper instead of p.

qs.s: An SSR e-commerce page scores 95 in Lighthouse on a laptop, but field data shows INP of 450 ms on Android. The page ships 900 KB of JS that hydrates the whole tree. Best first step?
o: Add a CDN in front of the HTML
Reduce what hydrates: make static sections Server Components and lazy-load heavy widgets
Turn off SSR and use CSR
Add suppressHydrationWarning to the root
qs.e: INP suffers because hydration and JS execution keep the main thread busy. A CDN improves TTFB, not interactivity. CSR still runs the same JS. Suppressing warnings changes nothing about the cost.

qs.s: A dev fixes a theme-flash bug by reading localStorage.theme directly inside a component's render, guarded by typeof window !== 'undefined'. What happens on hydration?
o: Server renders the default theme, the browser renders the saved theme on first render, so React reports a mismatch
It works, because the guard prevents errors
localStorage is readable on the server in Next.js
React waits for localStorage before hydrating
qs.e: The guard avoids a crash on the server but creates two different outputs. The usual fix is a cookie read on the server, or a tiny inline script that sets a class on <html> before paint plus suppressHydrationWarning on that one element.

qs.s: Read this client component. What happens when a phone user loads the server-rendered page?

code.title: Nav.tsx

o: It works: the guard makes the server and client agree
The server renders DesktopNav, the phone's first render returns MobileNav, so hydration fails and React re-renders that part on the client, with a visible flicker
The server crashes with “window is not defined”
React keeps the server HTML and only patches the changed class names
qs.e: The guard prevents the server crash but creates two different outputs. React 19 does not patch mismatches; it throws the server HTML away up to the nearest Suspense boundary. For layout differences use CSS media queries (render both, hide one); for real data use useSyncExternalStore with a server snapshot or update after mount.

qs.s: Why does this hook pass a third argument, () => true?

code.title: useOnline.ts

o: It is the default value when navigator is undefined in old browsers
It tells React how often to poll for changes
It is the server snapshot: React uses it on the server and during hydration, so the first client render matches the HTML; then React re-renders with the real browser value
It forces the hook to skip SSR entirely
qs.e: getServerSnapshot is used both on the server and for the hydration render, which keeps them identical. Right after hydration React checks the client snapshot and re-renders if it differs. Without it, any component using the hook during SSR throws an error.

qs.s: A page has the header and a long comments section, each inside its own <Suspense>. While React is still hydrating, the user clicks “Like” inside the comments, which are not hydrated yet. What does React 18/19 do?
o: It hydrates the comments boundary first (it gets priority because the user interacted with it) and then replays the click
The click is lost; the user must click again after hydration
React hydrates in document order and queues the click until the whole page is done
The browser follows the button's default action and reloads the page
qs.e: This is selective hydration. Suspense boundaries hydrate independently, and a discrete event like a click raises the priority of the boundary it hit. It only works when the page is split into boundaries: one giant tree must hydrate fully before anything responds.

qs.s: An Astro product page has slow INP during load. Which change fixes it with the least risk?

code.title: product.astro
code.src:
---
import Gallery from '../components/Gallery.tsx';   // above the fold
import ChatWidget from '../components/Chat.tsx';    // footer, 180 KB
---
<Gallery client:load />
<main>...</main>
<ChatWidget client:load />

o: Remove client:load from both components
Change Gallery to client:only
Move both components into one big React island so they share React
Change the chat to client:visible (or client:idle) so its JS loads and hydrates only when needed; keep client:load on the gallery
qs.e: client:load hydrates immediately and competes with the important gallery. Delaying the footer widget removes 180 KB of startup work. Removing the directive renders static HTML with no interactivity, so the chat would be broken. One big island hydrates more, not less.

interview.q: What exactly happens during hydration in React 19, and what happens on a mismatch?
answer: hydrateRoot renders the client components again and walks the existing DOM, claiming nodes and attaching event listeners instead of creating elements.
Suspense boundaries hydrate as separate units; React prioritises a boundary the user interacts with and replays the event (selective hydration).
On a mismatch React does not patch: it reports a recoverable error (onRecoverableError) and client-renders up to the nearest Suspense boundary, or the whole root.
React 19 tolerates extra tags in <head>/<body> from extensions and third-party scripts, and shows a diff of the mismatch in dev.
suppressHydrationWarning only works one level deep and is for unavoidable text like timestamps.
followups: How would you find which component causes a mismatch that only happens in production?
Why can invalid HTML nesting cause a mismatch when the code is deterministic?

interview.q: Our SSR page has an INP of 400 ms on Android. How do you investigate and reduce hydration cost?
answer: Confirm it is load-time INP: RUM attribution shows long input delay on early interactions, and a throttled trace shows long tasks from hydration.
Reduce what hydrates: convert static parts to Server Components, push 'use client' down to leaves, delete unused client libraries.
Split hydration: wrap independent sections in <Suspense> so they hydrate in chunks and selective hydration can prioritise clicks.
Delay non-critical widgets (chat, ads, below-the-fold carousels) with lazy, on visibility or idle.
Remove third-party scripts that compete on the main thread during startup, and check that no hydration mismatches force double renders.
followups: What metric tells you hydration is the problem, not event handlers?
When would you consider islands or a different framework instead?

interview.q: Compare islands (Astro), React Server Components and resumability (Qwik). When would you pick each?
answer: Islands: the page is static HTML and only marked components hydrate, each on its own trigger. Great for content sites with a few widgets; harder for app-like pages with shared state.
RSC: the server parts never ship JS and the client parts hydrate; good for apps that need rich interactivity and server data in one React tree.

Resumability: the framework serialises state and listeners into the HTML and loads code only for the handler that runs, so there is almost no startup hydration; the cost is a different programming model and a smaller ecosystem.
Choose by page type and team: content-heavy → islands; React product app → RSC; extreme startup constraints and a team willing to adopt a new model → resumability.
followups: What does an RSC app still hydrate that an islands site would not?
How do islands share state with each other?

one: Components that run only on the server (or at build), can read data directly, and send rendered output with zero component JS to the browser.
an: Some furniture arrives fully assembled and bolted down (server components); only the pieces with moving parts ship as kits (client components).
how: In the Next.js App Router, components are server by default. They can be async and query the DB or call services directly. Their code never reaches the client.
'use client' marks a boundary: that component and everything it imports ship JS and can use state, effects and browser APIs. Client components still pre-render to HTML on the server.

Props crossing the boundary must be serialisable by React: primitives, plain objects, arrays, Date, Map, Set, Promises, JSX and Server Functions are allowed; normal functions and class instances are not.
Server Functions ('use server') let client code call server code like RPC; when used for a form action or mutation they are called Server Actions. Each one is a public POST endpoint.
why: Reduces bundle size and removes many API endpoints and client-side fetch waterfalls.
trade: A new mental model: what runs where, caching semantics, and security (Server Actions are public endpoints; validate and authorize inside them).

myth.m: 'use client' means the component only renders on the client.
myth.r: Client components still pre-render on the server for the initial HTML. The directive means "this also ships JS and hydrates".

React Server Components run only on the server. They can read the database directly, and their code is never sent to the browser. Only their rendered result is sent.

Marked 'use client'; ships JS and can be interactive.

prod.summary: In production, RSC moves data access and secrets onto the server, which is great for bundle size and dangerous for security. Seniors check three things: nothing secret leaks into a client component, every Server Action authenticates and validates like an API route, and the React/Next.js versions are patched (the RSC protocol had a CVSS 10.0 remote-code-execution bug in December 2025, followed by several denial-of-service and source-exposure fixes up to January 2026).
checklist: Every 'use server' function checks session, ownership and input (Zod or similar) inside the function. UI hiding is not access control.
Server-only modules (DB client, secrets) import 'server-only', so an accidental client import fails the build.
Server Components pass only the fields the client needs (a DTO), not the whole DB row with passwordHash or internal flags.
Auth is checked close to the data (in the page/action/data layer), not only in proxy.ts (Next.js 16's rename of middleware.ts).
react, react-dom, react-server-dom-* and next are on the latest patch of their line; Dependabot/Renovate alerts for them are treated as urgent.
Secrets are read inside the Server Action body, not captured from the surrounding component: closed-over values travel to the client and back (encrypted by Next.js, but still outside the server).
'use client' sits on small leaf components; check the client bundle for large libraries that should have stayed on the server.
Mutations call updateTag/revalidateTag/revalidatePath so the UI does not show stale data after a write.
numbers: CVE-2025-55182 (“React2Shell”, CVSS 10.0): pre-auth RCE via the RSC Flight protocol in react-server-dom-* 19.0.0, 19.1.0, 19.1.1 and 19.2.0; first fixed in 19.0.1, 19.1.2 and 19.2.1.

Follow-up RSC bugs (denial of service CVE-2025-55184, CVE-2025-67779, CVE-2026-23864; source code exposure CVE-2025-55183) mean the fully patched versions are 19.0.4, 19.1.5 and 19.2.4 or later (January 2026).
CVE-2025-29927 (CVSS 9.1): Next.js middleware could be skipped with an x-middleware-subrequest header; fixed in 15.2.3, 14.2.25, 13.5.9 and 12.3.5.
Next.js Server Actions accept request bodies up to 1 MB by default (serverActions.bodySizeLimit).
Next.js 16 proxy.ts runs on the Node.js runtime only; the Edge runtime is not supported there.
failures: Security report: anyone can delete any post with a crafted POST request.
The Server Action trusted the postId from the client and only the UI hid the button. Inside the action: get the session, load the post, compare authorId, validate input, then delete.

The client bundle suddenly contains the Prisma client or an API key name.
A 'use client' file imported a shared module that also imports the DB. Split the module, and add import 'server-only' to the DB file so this fails at build time.
“Only plain objects can be passed to Client Components from Server Components.”
A class instance (e.g. an ORM model or a Decimal) or a normal function was passed as a prop. Map it to a plain object, or pass a Server Function instead of a callback.
Protected pages were reachable even though middleware checked the cookie.
Auth lived only in middleware (CVE-2025-29927 showed it can be bypassed). Upgrade, and verify the session again in the data access layer for every protected read and write.

Disable JavaScript in the client bundle

interview.q: What is the difference between Server Components and SSR? Why do we need both?
answer: SSR turns a component tree into HTML for the first load; the same components still ship JS and hydrate.
Server Components are a component type that only ever runs on the server; their output is the RSC payload (Flight), and their code never ships.
In Next.js both happen: Server Components produce the RSC payload, then client components are SSR-ed to HTML from it, and the browser hydrates only the client components.
On client navigation there is no HTML: the router fetches only the RSC payload for the new route and merges it, keeping client state.
Benefit: less JS and direct data access. Cost: a serialisation boundary, new caching rules and new security surface (Server Actions).

interview.q: How do you secure Server Actions in a Next.js 16 app?
answer: Treat every action as a public POST endpoint: anyone can call it with any arguments.
Inside each action: authenticate, authorise against the resource (ownership, role), validate input with a schema, then act. Put this in a shared data access layer so it is not forgotten.
Do not rely on proxy.ts alone (CVE-2025-29927 showed middleware can be bypassed); check auth near the data.
Return only safe error messages; avoid capturing secrets in closures; use server-only for secret modules and React taint APIs for sensitive values.
Rate-limit expensive actions, keep the body size limit small, and keep React/Next.js on the latest patch (React2Shell and its follow-ups were in the protocol itself).

Make only interactive leaves client components: add-to-cart button, image carousel, variant picker. Pass server-rendered content into them as children instead of importing it.

t: State management: server vs client state
one: Separate data owned by the server (cached copies of backend data) from data owned by the UI (open modals, form drafts, selected tab). Different tools fit each.
an: Server state is a borrowed library book: you hold a copy that might be outdated and must be returned or refreshed. Client state is your own notebook.
how: Server state: TanStack Query, SWR, RTK Query, Apollo, or framework loaders. They handle caching, deduping, refetching, stale times, optimistic updates and invalidation.
Client state: local useState first; lift up when shared; context for rarely changing values (theme, user); a small store (Zustand, Jotai, Redux Toolkit, signals) for complex shared UI state.
URL state: filters, tabs, pagination belong in the URL so they survive refresh and can be shared.
Derive instead of duplicating: computed values should not be stored as separate state.
why: Most "we need Redux" pain is server state managed by hand. Splitting the two removes huge amounts of code and bugs.
trade: Global stores make everything accessible and therefore coupled. Keep state as local as possible.

myth.m: Big apps need one global store for everything.
myth.r: Most state is either server cache or local. A global store is for the genuinely shared UI remainder.

q.s: A team stores API responses in Redux, writes loading/error flags by hand, and has stale data bugs after mutations. Best move?
o: Add more reducers
Move server data to a query cache (TanStack Query/SWR) with invalidation after mutations
Put it in localStorage
Use context everywhere
q.e: Server-cache libraries solve loading, dedupe, staleness and refetch as a solved problem.

lab: Rewrite a page that uses useEffect + useState for fetching with TanStack Query; delete the hand-written loading/error code.
Move a list's filters into the URL search params and confirm refresh and share keep them.

plain:
Most “state” in an app is actually one of two very different things. Server state: data that lives on the server and you hold a copy of (users, orders). It can become out of date. Client state: data that only exists in the UI (is the modal open, which tab is selected, what the user typed).

Using the right tool for each removes a lot of code and bugs.
bridge: If your Redux store is mostly API responses plus isLoading and error flags you manage by hand, you are managing server state with a client state tool.

walk.title: Simplifying an orders page
steps: Before: Redux slice with orders, loading, error, thunks to fetch, manual refetch after creating an order. About 150 lines, with stale data bugs.
Move server data to TanStack Query: useQuery({ queryKey: ['orders'], queryFn: fetchOrders }). Loading, errors, caching and refetch are handled.
After creating an order: queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] }). The list updates.
Move the filters (status, page) into the URL search params, so refresh and sharing keep them.
What is left for client state: whether the “new order” dialog is open, a useState. The slice is deleted.

terms: A cached copy of data owned by the server.
Data that exists only in the UI.
State stored in the address (path, query params).
Marking cached server data as stale so it refetches.
Values calculated from other state instead of stored.
insights: When a bug report says “the list did not update”, check query keys and invalidation first, not the components.
Before adding a global store, list what will go in it. If most items are API data, you need a query cache instead.
Two copies of the same data will disagree sooner or later. Keep one source and derive the rest.

prod.summary: In production apps, most state bugs are cache bugs: stale lists after a mutation, duplicate requests, or the same data stored in three places. Seniors split server state (query cache with clear keys and invalidation), URL state (filters, page) and small local UI state, and they choose staleTime deliberately instead of accepting the defaults.
checklist: Server data lives in one query cache (TanStack Query, SWR, RTK Query or framework loaders), not copied into Redux/Zustand.
Query keys include every input of the request (['orders', { status, page }]), so different filters never share a cache entry.
Every mutation invalidates or updates the affected keys; optimistic updates have a rollback in onError.
staleTime is set per query based on how fast the data changes; the default of 0 refetches on every mount and window focus.
Filters, sort, tab and pagination are in the URL search params, so refresh, back button and shared links work.
No derived values stored as state (totals, filtered lists); compute them during render or with a selector.
Global client stores hold only truly shared UI state (theme, auth snapshot, multi-step wizard).
numbers: TanStack Query v5 defaults: staleTime 0, gcTime 5 minutes (unused cache removed after that), 3 retries with exponential backoff.
TanStack Query refetches stale queries on window focus, on mount and on reconnect by default.
cacheTime was renamed to gcTime in TanStack Query v5.
failures: After creating an order, the list still shows the old orders until the user refreshes.
The mutation does not invalidate the list. Add onSettled: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] }); the prefix key also refreshes every filtered variant.
The API gets 5 requests every time a user switches browser tabs.
Default staleTime: 0 plus refetchOnWindowFocus and five components using the query. Set a realistic staleTime (e.g. 30 s) for data that does not change every second.
Changing the status filter shows the previous filter's data for a moment, then the wrong page.
The filter is not in the query key, so all filters share one cache entry. Put every request input in the key.
Users lose their filters when they press Back or share a link.
Filters live in useState. Move them to URL search params and read them as the source of truth.
The whole app re-renders on every keystroke in a search box.
Input text is stored in a global context that many components read. Keep it local, and debounce before writing to the URL or query key.

gcTime is too short
The query key should be a string, not an array
qs.e: Simultaneous identical requests are deduplicated, but with staleTime: 0 the data is stale immediately, so later mounts and focus events trigger new fetches. Set a staleTime that matches how fast the data changes.

Move both into Redux
Add total to the effect's dependency array
Store total in a ref
qs.e: total is derived state. Storing it causes an extra render and can be out of sync for one frame. Calculating it from items removes a whole class of bugs.

qs.s: A user types “re”, then quickly “react”. Sometimes the list shows results for “re”. Why?

code.title: Search.tsx

o: React batches the two state updates and keeps the first one
useEffect does not run again when q changes quickly
The browser caches the first response
A race: the request for “re” is slower and finishes last, overwriting the newer results. Abort or ignore stale responses in the effect cleanup, or use a query library keyed by q
qs.e: Responses can arrive in any order. Without cleanup, the last one to finish wins, not the last one sent. Use an AbortController (or an ignore flag) in the cleanup, or TanStack Query, where each q has its own cache entry and only the current key renders.

qs.s: After upgrading to Zustand v5, this component crashes with “Maximum update depth exceeded”. Why?

code.title: CartBadge.tsx

o: The selector returns a new object on every call, so the store snapshot never looks stable and React keeps re-rendering. Use useShallow or select each value separately
Zustand v5 does not support selectors
s.items.length must be wrapped in useMemo
The store must be created with createContext in v5
qs.e: Zustand v5 relies on React's useSyncExternalStore, which compares snapshots with Object.is. A fresh object every time means “changed” every time, which loops. useShallow compares the fields instead. Selecting primitives one by one also works.

qs.s: A “Like” button uses React 19 useOptimistic inside a form action. The Server Action fails with a 500. What does the user see after the action finishes?
o: The optimistic “liked” state stays until the page reloads
React shows the closest error boundary for the whole page
The optimistic value is dropped and the button shows the real (not liked) state again; you should also show an error message
The optimistic update is retried three times automatically
qs.e: useOptimistic only shows the optimistic value while the action or transition is pending. When it ends, the hook goes back to the real state you passed in. Because nothing changed on the server, the like disappears. Showing why (a toast, useActionState error) is your job.

qs.s: TanStack Query v5 with staleTime: 60_000 and the default gcTime. A user opens /orders, goes to another page for 3 minutes, then comes back. What happens?
o: A loading spinner, because the cache was cleared after 1 minute
The cached orders appear instantly, and a background refetch starts because the data is stale
The cached orders appear and no request is made, because the data is still fresh
An error, because the query was garbage-collected
qs.e: staleTime (60 s) decides when data is old; gcTime (default 5 minutes) decides when an unused entry is deleted. After 3 minutes the data is stale but still in the cache: instant render plus background refresh. After more than 5 minutes away, the entry would be gone and the user would see a loading state.

interview.q: How do you decide where a piece of state should live?
answer: First ask who owns it. Data owned by the server goes in a query cache (TanStack Query, SWR, RSC/loaders), never copied into a client store.
If it should survive refresh or be shareable (filters, tab, page, selected item), it goes in the URL.
If one component uses it, keep it local; lift it only to the closest common parent of the components that need it.
Form drafts: in the form (uncontrolled inputs, form libraries, useActionState), not in a global store.
Only truly cross-cutting client state (theme, auth snapshot, a multi-step wizard, an editor document) goes in context or a small store with selectors.
Never store derived values; compute them.
followups: When does context become a performance problem, and what do you do then?
Where would you keep the state of a complex drag-and-drop board?

interview.q: How would you implement optimistic updates safely, including errors and two mutations in a row?
answer: Cancel in-flight queries for the key so a slow refetch cannot overwrite the optimistic value.
Snapshot the previous data, apply the change, return the snapshot as context; restore it in onError and show an error.
Invalidate in onSettled so the cache re-syncs with the server either way.
With concurrent mutations, rollback to an old snapshot can undo a newer success; prefer invalidating only when no other mutation on the key is running (isMutating), or apply per-item patches.
Use optimistic UI only where failure is rare and easy to undo (likes, toggles), not for payments.
In React 19 forms, useOptimistic + a Server Action gives automatic revert when the action ends.
followups: How do you make the server mutation idempotent if the client retries?
How would you show optimistic items in a paginated list?

interview.q: In 2026, with RSC and query caches, when do you still choose Redux Toolkit or Zustand?
answer: When there is real client-owned, shared, complex state: editors, canvases, offline-first apps, multi-step flows with undo/redo.
When many components read slices of fast-changing state and need fine-grained subscriptions (selectors) instead of context re-renders.
Redux Toolkit when you want strict patterns, devtools time travel and middleware in a large team; Zustand or Jotai when you want minimal API.
Not for server data: RTK Query or TanStack Query handle that; a hand-written slice with loading flags is a smell.
With RSC, much page data never reaches client state at all, so the store gets smaller, not bigger.
followups: How would you migrate a large Redux app that stores API data in slices?

one: How source modules become the files the browser downloads, and how to make them smaller and loaded only when needed.
an: Packing for a trip. Tree shaking leaves unused items at home. Code splitting packs separate bags so you only carry the one you need today.
how: Bundlers (Vite with Rolldown since Vite 8, Turbopack as the Next.js 16 default, webpack, Rspack, esbuild) resolve imports, transform TS/JSX, and output optimised chunks.

Tree shaking drops unused exports. Needs ES modules and side-effect-free packages ("sideEffects": false in package.json); CommonJS libraries like classic lodash cannot be shaken, so use lodash-es or per-function imports.
Code splitting: dynamic import() and route-level chunks load code on demand. Lazy-load heavy, rarely used components (editors, charts, maps).
Measure with a bundle analyzer; set a budget in CI.
why: JS is the most expensive byte on the web: it must be downloaded, parsed, compiled and executed, which hits mid-range phones hardest.
trade: Too many tiny chunks add request overhead and waterfalls. Split by route and by heavy feature, not by every component.

myth.r: Minifying 2MB of JS still leaves a lot. Not shipping code at all is the real win.

q.s: A date library adds 300KB to every page but is only used on the reports screen. Fix?
o: Minify harder
Dynamically import it on the reports route, or replace with a lighter library
Inline it
Serve it over HTTP/1.1
q.e: Load heavy code only where it is used.

more: Barrel files and why they hurt tree shaking
lab: Run vite build with rollup-plugin-visualizer (or Next's bundle analyzer) on one of your apps. Find the three largest modules.
Lazy-load the heaviest route-level component and compare initial JS size before and after.
docs: web.dev: Reduce JavaScript payloads with code splitting

plain: A bundler takes your many source files and dependencies and produces the files the browser downloads. Two main ways to make them smaller: tree shaking (dropping code you never use) and code splitting (loading code only when it is needed, like when the user opens a specific page).
bridge: Vite, Next.js (Turbopack/webpack) and esbuild are bundlers. React.lazy(() => import('./Editor')) is code splitting.

walk.title: Shrinking a slow first load
steps: First load downloads 1.2 MB of JS. The bundle analyzer shows: a charting library (400 KB), a rich text editor (300 KB), and a date library (70 KB).
Charts are only on the reports page → lazy-load them with dynamic import().
The editor only appears when you click “Write post” → lazy-load it on click.
The date library is imported as a whole → switch to per-function imports or a smaller library.
First load becomes about 440 KB. Reports and the editor load in a second when needed.

terms: An output JS file / one piece of a split bundle.
Removing unused exports at build time.
Loading parts of the app on demand.
A tool that shows what takes space in your bundles.
insights: Ask “how much JS runs before the first click works?” per route, not “how big is the bundle?” for the whole app.
Bundle growth usually comes from one innocent import in a shared file (layout, utils, providers). Review imports there carefully.
Splitting moves the cost, it does not remove it. Preload a lazy chunk on hover or focus so the user does not wait after the click.

prod.summary: In production, bundle size is a performance budget with an owner. Seniors know the size of the initial JS for each important route, block PRs that grow it without a reason, and look for the usual suspects: a heavy library in a shared chunk, barrel files that defeat tree shaking, polyfills for browsers you do not support, and source maps or dev code shipped by mistake.
checklist: A CI budget (size-limit, bundlewatch or Lighthouse CI) fails the PR when initial JS for key routes grows past the agreed limit.
The bundle analyzer is run before release; the top 5 modules are known and justified.
Heavy features (editor, charts, maps, PDF) load via dynamic import() and are preloaded on user intent (hover/focus).
Imports avoid barrel files of huge libraries (import { X } from 'icons' that pulls 2,000 icons); use direct paths or a bundler option like Next.js optimizePackageImports.
The browser target matches real users; you do not ship ES5 polyfills to browsers that support ES2020+.
Source maps are uploaded to error tracking but not publicly served, or you accept that your source is readable.
Long-term caching works: chunk file names contain a content hash, and are served with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.
numbers: Vite 8 (stable March 2026) uses Rolldown as its single bundler, replacing the esbuild + Rollup combination.
Next.js 16 uses Turbopack by default for next dev and next build; a custom webpack config makes next build fail unless you pass --webpack.
Next.js 16's default browser support is Chrome/Edge/Firefox 111+ and Safari 16.4+.
failures: Initial JS jumped from 250 KB to 900 KB after a small PR.

A shared component started importing a chart library at the top level, so it moved into the common chunk. Load the chart with dynamic import() and add a CI size budget so this fails in review next time.
Users get “ChunkLoadError: Loading chunk 123 failed” right after a deploy.
Open tabs still reference old chunk names that the new deploy deleted. Keep old assets for some days (immutable, hashed files) and, on this error, reload the page once.
Importing one icon adds 600 KB.
The icon package's index re-exports everything (barrel file) and is not marked side-effect-free. Import from the icon's own path or enable package import optimisation.
next build fails after upgrading to Next.js 16 with a message about a webpack configuration.
Turbopack is the default and a plugin adds a webpack option. Migrate the plugin to Turbopack options, or build with next build --webpack for now.

code.title: Lazy-load a heavy editor and preload it on intent
code.note: Calling loadEditor() early starts the download; the module system caches it, so lazy reuses the same promise when the user clicks.

qs.s: You import { debounce } from 'lodash' and the analyzer shows ~70 KB of lodash in the bundle. You are using a modern bundler with tree shaking on. Why?
o: Tree shaking only works in development
The bundler cannot shake debounce because it is a function
lodash is published as CommonJS, which bundlers cannot tree-shake reliably; use lodash-es or lodash/debounce
Minification is turned off
qs.e: Tree shaking depends on static ES module imports and exports. A CommonJS package is treated as one block. Switching to an ESM build or a per-function import fixes it.

qs.s: A team splits every component into its own lazy chunk. The home page now makes 140 JS requests and LCP got worse. What happened?
o: Too many small chunks create request overhead and loading waterfalls (chunk A loads, then discovers chunk B)
HTTP/2 does not support more than 100 requests
Lazy loading disables caching
The CDN compresses small files badly
qs.e: Splitting has a cost. Split by route and by heavy, rarely used features. Components needed for the first view should be in the initial chunk.

qs.s: After each deploy, Sentry shows a burst of “ChunkLoadError” for about an hour, then it stops. What is the most likely cause?
o: The new build has a syntax error
Users with tabs open from the previous version request old hashed chunks that no longer exist on the server
The CDN is down
Tree shaking removed a needed module
qs.e: Old pages still reference old file names. Keep previous assets available for a while and handle the error with a one-time reload. A real syntax error would not stop after an hour.

qs.s: Your design system package added the field below. After the next release, apps that bundle it with webpack lose all button styles, and the CSS file in their build output no longer has the button rules. Why?

code.title: packages/ui/package.json

o: exports hides the CSS files from the bundler
dist/index.js contains import './styles.css'; with sideEffects: false the bundler may drop imports that bind nothing, so the CSS import is removed. Use "sideEffects": ["**/*.css"]
Production builds minify CSS class names
The CSS is loaded but with lower specificity
qs.e: sideEffects: false promises that importing a file for its effects alone is never needed. A CSS import is exactly such an effect, so webpack drops import './styles.css', in development and production builds alike. List the files that do have side effects (CSS, polyfills) instead of false. Not every bundler reacts the same way: esbuild and Vite keep CSS imports anyway, which is why the bug can show up in one app and not in another.

qs.s: Read this bundle analyzer excerpt. What is the problem and the first fix?

code.title: analyzer: main chunk (parsed size)

o: date-fns is not tree-shakable; replace it with moment
The analyzer counts the same file twice; nothing to fix

Two major versions of date-fns are bundled because a dependency needs an older one. Upgrade the dependency or align versions (pnpm overrides only if the APIs are compatible), then check the analyzer again
Move date-fns to devDependencies
qs.e: Package managers install a second copy when version ranges do not overlap, and the bundler includes both. Duplicates are common after upgrades. moment is larger and not tree-shakable. devDependencies does not change what the bundle imports.

qs.s: Your CI budget reports the main route: 170 KB gzip, 610 KB uncompressed. A teammate says “only 170 KB matters”. What is the better view?
o: Both matter: the compressed size sets download time, but the phone must parse, compile and execute the full 610 KB, which is the main cost on mid-range devices
Only the uncompressed size matters, because browsers download uncompressed JS
Only the gzip size matters, because CPUs are fast enough
Neither; only the number of requests matters on HTTP/2
qs.e: Compression helps the network only. After download the engine works on the full source text, so CPU time scales with uncompressed size. That is why JS costs more than an image of the same byte size. Track both in the budget.

qs.s: After upgrading Next.js, the build fails on this file. What is the correct fix?

code.title: app/map/page.tsx (Server Component)

o: Replace next/dynamic with React.lazy in the same file
Remove ssr: false and guard window inside Map with typeof window
Add export const dynamic = 'force-static'
Move the dynamic(..., { ssr: false }) call into a small 'use client' component and render that from the page
qs.e: ssr: false is not allowed in Server Components, because “skip server rendering” only makes sense for a client component. A client wrapper keeps the map out of the server render and in its own chunk. Removing ssr: false would server-render a component that touches window.

interview.q: Initial JS doubled in a release. Walk me through finding and fixing it.
answer: Compare the analyzer output (or the CI budget report) of the two builds and find which chunk grew and which modules are new.

Typical causes: a heavy library imported at the top of a shared component, a barrel file import, a duplicate dependency version, a polyfill or a changed browser target, a dev-only module in production.
Use git log on the PR range plus pnpm why to find who pulls the module in.
Fix: dynamic import() for heavy features, direct imports instead of barrels, dedupe versions, or a lighter library.
Prevent: a size budget per key route that fails the PR, with an owner who can approve exceptions.
followups: What is the difference between parsed, gzip and stat size in the analyzer?
How do you decide between replacing a library and lazy-loading it?

interview.q: How does tree shaking actually work, and what breaks it?
answer: The bundler builds the module graph from static import/export statements, marks which exports are used, and drops the rest during minification.
It needs ES modules: CommonJS (require, module.exports) is dynamic, so the whole module is usually kept.
Side effects block it: code that runs on import (polyfills, CSS, top-level calls) must be kept unless sideEffects says it is safe to drop.
Barrel files make every import touch every module; with side effects or poor analysis they pull in everything.
Dynamic property access on a namespace (lib[name]) and class-based APIs with static members limit what can be removed.
followups: What does the /*#__PURE__*/ annotation do?
Why can a package be tree-shakable in Vite but not in an older webpack setup?

interview.q: What is your code-splitting strategy for a large React/Next.js app, and how do you avoid loading waterfalls?
answer: Route-level splitting first (frameworks do it automatically), then split heavy, rarely used features (editors, charts, maps, PDF).
Do not split what the first view needs; that only adds a request and delays render.
Avoid waterfalls: preload on intent (hover, focus, viewport), let the framework prefetch routes, and avoid chains where chunk A loads before it discovers chunk B.
Share common vendor code in stable chunks with content hashes for long-term caching.
Measure the effect on INP/LCP, not just bytes: more chunks can make things slower.
followups: How do you handle a chunk that fails to load after a deploy?
When would you inline a small dependency instead of sharing it?

t: How the browser renders a page
one: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, combined into a render tree, then layout (geometry), paint (pixels) and composite (layers to screen).
an: An assembly line: read the plan, measure every room, paint the walls, then stack transparent sheets into the final picture.
how: CSS and synchronous scripts in the head are render-blocking. Use defer/async, inline critical CSS, preload key fonts and the LCP image.

Changing geometry (width, top) triggers layout for affected elements; changing colour triggers paint; changing transform/opacity can be done by the compositor alone, which is why they animate smoothly.
Layout thrashing: reading layout (offsetHeight) after writing styles in a loop forces repeated synchronous layouts.
The main thread does JS, style, layout and paint. A 300ms JS task freezes everything, including input handling.
why: This pipeline explains nearly all frontend performance advice and every Web Vitals fix.
trade: will-change and extra layers speed animation but cost GPU memory. Use sparingly.

myth.m: Animating left/top is as smooth as transform.
myth.r: left/top trigger layout every frame. transform can skip layout and paint entirely.

q.s: A sidebar animation janks on low-end phones. It animates width. Better approach?
o: Animate margin
Animate transform: translateX (and opacity) so the compositor handles it
Use setInterval
Add more JS
q.e: Compositor-only properties avoid layout and paint on every frame.

lab: Record a Performance trace while animating width vs transform; compare the purple (layout) and green (paint) blocks.
Write a loop that reads offsetHeight and writes styles for 1,000 elements; then batch reads before writes and compare.

plain:
To show a page, the browser goes through a pipeline: read HTML into the DOM, read CSS, work out the size and position of every element (layout), fill in the pixels (paint), and stack layers together (composite).

Changing some CSS properties re-runs the whole pipeline; others (transform, opacity) only need the last cheap step. That is why some animations are smooth and others stutter.
bridge: In DevTools Performance, purple blocks are layout, green are paint. If you see lots of purple during an animation, you are animating a property that triggers layout.

walk.title: Fixing a janky sidebar animation
steps: The sidebar opens by animating width from 0 to 300px.
Every frame, width changes → the browser recalculates layout for the sidebar and all content next to it → repaints → composites.
On a cheap phone, that takes more than 16 ms per frame, so the animation stutters.
Change to animating transform: translateX(-300px) → translateX(0).
Transform does not change layout. The compositor (often on the GPU) moves the already-painted layer, so the animation stays smooth at 60 fps.

terms: The browser's in-memory trees of HTML and CSS.
Combining layers into the final image, often on the GPU.
Resources that stop the first paint until they load.
insights: Before fixing performance, find the slow step in a Performance trace: script, style, layout, paint or composite. Each has a different fix.
At 60 Hz a frame is about 16 ms, and the browser needs part of it for its own work. Your JS per frame should stay well below that.
The cheapest rendering work is work the browser can skip: off-screen content, unchanged layers, layout that does not change.

prod.summary: In production, rendering performance shows up as LCP (how fast the main content appears), CLS (how much it jumps) and INP (how fast it responds). Seniors read a DevTools Performance trace to find which pipeline step is slow: blocking resources before first paint, long JavaScript tasks, forced layouts, or expensive paints, and then fix that step instead of guessing.
checklist: The LCP image is in the HTML (not injected by JS), has fetchpriority="high", and is not lazy-loaded.
Images and embeds have width/height or aspect-ratio, so they reserve space (no CLS).
Scripts use defer or type="module"; third-party tags load after the main content.
Web fonts are preloaded or self-hosted with font-display: swap (or optional) and a size-matched fallback to limit layout shift.
Animations use transform and opacity; no animated width, top, box-shadow on large areas.
No layout thrashing in loops: read all geometry first, then write styles (or use requestAnimationFrame).
Long lists or pages use virtualisation or content-visibility: auto so off-screen parts skip rendering.
numbers: At 60 Hz the browser has about 16.7 ms per frame for JS, style, layout, paint and composite together.
Chrome marks any main-thread task longer than 50 ms as a “long task”.
Core Web Vitals “good” thresholds at p75: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 (web.dev).
failures: Performance trace shows many purple “Layout” blocks with a red triangle and the warning “Forced reflow”.
Code reads offsetHeight/getBoundingClientRect() right after changing styles, in a loop. Batch all reads first, then all writes.
LCP is 4 s, but the hero image file is small.
The image is discovered late: it is a CSS background or is set by JS after hydration, or it has loading="lazy". Put an <img> in the server HTML with fetchpriority="high".
CLS of 0.25: the page jumps when the cookie banner and ads load.
Late content is inserted above existing content without reserved space. Reserve the slot size, or show banners as overlays that do not push content.
Scrolling a long table stutters; the trace shows long “Recalculate Style” steps.
Thousands of DOM nodes and complex selectors. Virtualise the list or add content-visibility: auto with contain-intrinsic-size.

code.title: Layout thrashing and the batched fix
code.note: With 1,000 cards the bad loop can trigger up to 1,000 layouts; the batched version triggers one. Often CSS can remove the JS completely.

qs.s: A trace of a slow page load shows the main thread idle for 1.5 s at the start, then a quick paint. The Network panel shows a 300 KB CSS file and two synchronous <script> tags in the <head>. What is delaying first paint?
o: Layout thrashing
Too many compositor layers
Slow paint of large images
Render-blocking resources: the browser waits for the CSS and the synchronous scripts before it can render
qs.e: An idle main thread followed by a fast paint means the browser is waiting on the network. Add defer to scripts, inline critical CSS, and load the rest later.

qs.s: A designer wants a card to grow with a soft shadow on hover. The implementation animates box-shadow and width; it janks on a list of 200 cards. Which version is smoothest?
o: Animate height instead of width
Animate transform: scale(), and fade in the shadow on a pseudo-element using opacity
Add will-change: width to all 200 cards
Use setInterval at 16 ms
qs.e: transform and opacity can be handled by the compositor. Shadow and size changes need paint/layout every frame. will-change on 200 elements wastes GPU memory and does not fix layout cost.

qs.s: A frame budget at 60 Hz is about 16.7 ms. Your scroll handler takes 9 ms and the browser needs about 6 ms for style, layout and paint. A new feature adds 4 ms of work to the handler. What happens?
o: Frames now take about 19 ms, so the browser misses frames and scrolling stutters
Nothing; the browser will run the handler on another thread
The browser reduces quality to fit in 16.7 ms
Only the first frame is affected
qs.e: 9 + 4 + 6 = 19 ms, over the budget, so frames are dropped. Fix by doing less per event (passive listeners, requestAnimationFrame throttling, IntersectionObserver instead of scroll math).

qs.s: Chrome DevTools shows this breakdown for the worst interaction on a product page. Which change gives the biggest INP win?

code.title: Performance panel: interaction
code.src:
Interaction: click on button “Add to cart”
  Input delay           12 ms
  Processing duration  380 ms   handleAddToCart → recalcCartTotals → setState
  Presentation delay    95 ms   Recalculate Style 60 ms, Layout 30 ms
INP: 487 ms

o: Reduce input delay by removing third-party scripts
Add will-change: transform to the cart icon
Shrink processing time: update the button state first, then yield (await scheduler.yield() or a transition) before the heavy total calculation, or move that calculation off the main thread
Serve the page from a CDN
qs.e: INP is input delay + processing + presentation delay. Processing is 380 of 487 ms, so that is where the win is. Yielding lets the browser paint the button's feedback before the slow work, and a worker or memoised calculation removes the work. Input delay is already small, and a CDN only affects loading.

qs.s: A site switched to a web font with font-display: swap. CLS rose to 0.12, mostly when the font arrives. Which fix targets the cause?

code.title: fonts.css

o: Add a fallback @font-face based on Arial with size-adjust, ascent-override and descent-override so the fallback text takes the same space (Next.js next/font generates this automatically), and preload the font
Change to font-display: block so text never changes
Add <link rel="preconnect"> to your own domain
Increase line-height on body
qs.e: The shift happens because the fallback and the web font have different metrics, so lines rewrap when the font swaps. Matching the fallback metrics removes the shift. block hides text for up to about 3 seconds (bad LCP and UX), and preconnecting to your own origin does nothing.

qs.s: You add .comment { content-visibility: auto; } to a page with 2,000 comments. Rendering is faster, but the scrollbar thumb jumps and the page “grows” while scrolling. Why?
o: content-visibility disables GPU compositing
Off-screen comments are laid out with zero height until they are rendered, because no contain-intrinsic-size was given; add one (e.g. contain-intrinsic-size: auto 120px)
The browser renders comments in random order
content-visibility only works on <section> elements
qs.e: Skipped elements use size containment, so without a placeholder size they count as 0 px tall, and the page height changes as they render. contain-intrinsic-size gives an estimate, and auto remembers the real size after the first render.

qs.s: This code reveals items as they scroll into view. With 500 items, scrolling stutters on phones. Best fix?

code.title: reveal.ts

o: Wrap the loop in setTimeout(..., 0)
Add { passive: true } to the listener; that removes the layout cost
Use offsetTop instead of getBoundingClientRect()
Use an IntersectionObserver: the browser reports visibility changes asynchronously, with no geometry reads in the scroll path and no forced layouts
qs.e: The handler runs on every scroll event and calls getBoundingClientRect() on all 500 items. After each classList.add, the next read forces a synchronous style recalculation (and a layout too, if the class changes size or position), so the work grows with the item count and sits right in the scroll path. IntersectionObserver computes intersections as part of the rendering pipeline and calls you only when visibility changes. passive helps only with listeners that could call preventDefault (touch, wheel); it does not make this loop cheaper. offsetTop forces layout just the same when layout is dirty.

interview.q: What happens between the browser receiving the first HTML bytes and the first pixel on screen?
answer: The parser builds the DOM incrementally; the preload scanner finds images, CSS and scripts early and starts downloading them.
CSS is render-blocking: the browser needs the CSSOM before it renders. Classic synchronous scripts are parser-blocking and also wait for preceding CSS.
Style calculation matches CSS rules to elements, layout computes geometry, paint records draw commands, and the compositor rasterises layers and puts them on screen.
To make it faster: small critical CSS, defer/type=module scripts, the LCP image in HTML with fetchpriority="high", fewer origins, fonts with preload and a matched fallback.
Measure with the Performance panel and the LCP sub-parts (TTFB, load delay, load time, render delay).
followups: Why does a <script> placed after a stylesheet wait for that stylesheet?
What can the preload scanner not find?

interview.q: How do you debug a poor INP that you only see in field data?
answer: Collect attribution in RUM (web-vitals attribution build): target element, interaction type, and the split into input delay, processing and presentation delay.
Use Long Animation Frame (LoAF) data to see which scripts ran during slow frames, including third-party ones.
Reproduce on a real mid-range Android or with 4–6× CPU throttling, recording the same interaction.
Fix by phase: input delay → break up startup and third-party long tasks; processing → less work in handlers, yield, workers; presentation → smaller DOM updates, less layout and style work.
Verify in the field after release; lab tools do not measure INP directly.
followups: Why is INP often worse during page load?
What does scheduler.yield() do differently from setTimeout(0)?

interview.q: When does an element get its own compositor layer, and what does that cost?
answer: Layers are created for things like 3D transforms, will-change: transform/opacity, video, canvas, fixed elements in some cases, and active transform/opacity animations.
Benefit: transform and opacity changes on that layer can run on the compositor thread without layout or paint, so they stay smooth even when the main thread is busy.
Cost: each layer uses GPU memory, and too many layers (layer explosion) slow down compositing, especially on phones.
Use will-change just before an animation and remove it after; check the Layers panel for unexpected layers.
followups: Why can an element that overlaps a layer become a layer too?
Is a CSS animation of transform still smooth if the main thread is blocked for 500 ms?
