one: Web Workers run JS on a background thread. Service workers are a programmable proxy between your page and the network, enabling offline support and caching.
an: A Web Worker is an assistant in a back room doing heavy calculations so the receptionist stays free. A service worker is a doorman who can answer from a stockroom when the street is closed.
how: Web Worker: new Worker(url), communicate via postMessage. No DOM access. Good for parsing big files, image processing, search indexing, crypto.
Service worker: registered once, intercepts fetch events for its scope, can serve from Cache Storage (offline), handle push notifications and background sync. Basis of PWAs.
Service workers have their own lifecycle: install → waiting (while tabs still use the old one) → activate. A bad one can keep serving stale assets until a new version activates.
why: Keeping the main thread free is how you get good INP for heavy apps. Offline capability matters for unreliable mobile networks.
trade: Workers add messaging complexity and copying costs for big data (transferables help). Service worker caching bugs are notoriously hard to debug, so ship a kill switch.

myth.m: async functions run on another thread.
myth.r: They run on the main thread. Only workers give real parallelism in the browser.

q.s: Parsing a 40MB CSV upload freezes the page for 6 seconds. Fix?
o: Make the parse function async
Parse in a Web Worker (streaming in chunks) and post results back
Use a service worker
Use CSS
q.e: Async does not move CPU work off the main thread; a worker does.

more: Service worker lifecycle and update flow
lab: Parse a big CSV in a Web Worker and post progress back; compare INP with main-thread parsing.
Add a service worker with Workbox that caches the app shell, then load the app offline (DevTools → Network → Offline).

plain:
A Web Worker runs JavaScript on a separate background thread, so heavy work does not freeze the page. It cannot touch the DOM; it talks to the page by sending messages.

A Service Worker is different: it sits between your page and the network, can answer requests from a cache, and makes offline mode and push notifications possible.
bridge: async functions do not run in the background; they still run on the main thread. A Web Worker is the only real way to run JS in parallel in the browser.

walk.title: Parsing a big file without freezing the page
steps: A user uploads a 40MB CSV. Parsing it on the main thread freezes the page for 6 seconds.
Create new Worker(new URL('./parse.worker.ts', import.meta.url)).
Send the file to the worker with postMessage(file).
The worker parses in chunks and sends progress messages; the page shows a progress bar and stays responsive.
When done, the worker sends the summary; the page renders it.

terms: Background thread for JS; no DOM access.
How the page and worker exchange data.
A network proxy script for caching, offline and push.
Progressive Web App: a website installable and usable offline, built with a service worker.
insights: A worker helps only when the work costs more than sending the data to it. For small tasks, the message overhead can be slower than doing the work inline.
Treat a service worker like a deployed server: it needs versioning, a rollout plan and a way to roll back.
Libraries like Comlink make worker calls look like normal async functions.

prod.summary: In production, Web Workers are the tool for keeping INP low when the app does real CPU work (parsing, search, image processing), and service workers are powerful but risky caches that can keep users on a broken version. Seniors measure the main-thread time saved, keep messages small (or transfer buffers), and always have an update and kill-switch plan for service workers.
checklist: CPU-heavy work over ~50 ms (parsing, diffing, compression, search indexing) runs in a worker, with progress messages to the UI.
Large binary data is sent as a transferable (postMessage(buf, [buf])) instead of being copied.
Workers are created once and reused (or pooled), not created per request.
The service worker script is served with Cache-Control: no-cache and has a versioned cache name; old caches are deleted in activate.
There is a tested kill switch: a no-op service worker that calls self.registration.unregister() and clears caches, deployable at the same URL.
HTML/navigation requests use network-first; only hashed static assets use cache-first.
The UI shows “New version available, reload” when a new service worker is waiting, instead of silent stale pages.
numbers: Browsers check for a new service worker script on navigation and at least once every 24 hours when an event fires.
By default a service worker's scope is the folder of its script; a wider scope needs the Service-Worker-Allowed response header.
A new service worker waits until all tabs using the old one are closed, unless it calls skipWaiting().
failures: After a deploy, some users keep seeing the old app for days, even after refreshing.

A cache-first service worker serves the old index.html, and the new worker is stuck in “waiting”. Serve HTML network-first, show an update prompt that calls skipWaiting(), and keep a kill-switch worker ready.
The page freezes for 3 s when the user pastes a big JSON document.
JSON.parse and validation run on the main thread. Move parsing into a worker and post back only the summary or the parsed result.
Moving work to a worker made it slower, and memory doubled.
A 200 MB ArrayBuffer is structured-cloned on each postMessage. Transfer it (postMessage(buf, [buf])) or stream it in chunks.
“ReferenceError: document is not defined” inside the worker.
Workers have no DOM. Send data back to the main thread and update the DOM there, or use OffscreenCanvas for drawing.

code.title: Streaming a large CSV in a Web Worker with progress
code.note: new URL(..., import.meta.url) is the pattern Vite, webpack and Turbopack recognise to bundle the worker as its own chunk.

qs.s: You move image filtering into a worker. Each frame you post a 30 MB ArrayBuffer to the worker and back. The UI is still slow. What is the cheapest fix?
o: Use two workers
Transfer the buffer instead of copying it: postMessage(buf, [buf])
Convert the buffer to a JSON string first
Use a service worker instead
qs.e: Structured cloning copies 30 MB twice per frame. Transferring moves ownership with no copy. JSON would be even slower, and a service worker is for network, not CPU work.

qs.s: Your PWA's service worker uses cache-first for all requests, including /index.html. You ship a critical bug fix. What do most returning users see?
o: The old version, until the new service worker activates and the cached HTML is replaced
The fix immediately, because the server has the new files
A browser error page
The fix, because browsers ignore service workers on reload
qs.e: Cache-first answers from the cache before asking the network. Navigation requests should be network-first, and the update flow (waiting worker, reload prompt) must be designed.

qs.s: A teammate says: “Our search filter takes 400 ms, so I wrapped it in async/await and Promise.resolve(). INP should be fine now.” What do you reply?
o: Correct, async code runs in parallel
Use setTimeout(fn, 0) instead; that runs on another thread
The work still runs on the main thread in one 400 ms task; move it to a worker or split it into smaller chunks that yield
INP does not measure JavaScript time
qs.e: Promises and timers only change when code runs, not where. A 400 ms task blocks input either way. A worker moves it off the main thread; chunking with scheduler.yield() or similar keeps each task short.

qs.s: Your service worker is below; its fetch handler (not shown) answers from the cache first. After a deploy, users with the app already open get errors when they open the Reports page (a lazy-loaded route). Why?

code.title: sw.js

o: clients.claim() reloads all open tabs, which loses their state
The new worker activates at once and deletes the old cache, but open tabs still run the old version and request old hashed chunks that are no longer cached (and maybe not on the server)
skipWaiting() must be called in activate, not in install
Cache names cannot contain version numbers
qs.e: Unconditional skipWaiting puts old pages under a new worker. The old page then asks for its old lazy chunks, which the new worker just deleted. Safer: wait, or call skipWaiting only when the user accepts “Reload to update”, and keep old assets available for a while. clients.claim() does not reload pages.

qs.s: You want to share a large buffer between the page and a worker without copying. In production you see this error. What is missing?

code.title: console
code.src:
Uncaught ReferenceError: SharedArrayBuffer is not defined
> self.crossOriginIsolated
false

o: The worker must be created with { type: 'module' }
You must import Atomics first
SharedArrayBuffer only works inside service workers

The page is not cross-origin isolated: serve it with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp (or credentialless), and make sure third-party resources still load
qs.e: After Spectre, browsers only expose SharedArrayBuffer in cross-origin isolated pages. The headers are the fix, but COEP blocks cross-origin resources that do not opt in (CORP/CORS), so test ads, embeds and CDNs. Often transferring an ArrayBuffer is enough and needs no headers.

qs.s: A photo app creates a new Web Worker for each of 60 selected images to resize them “in parallel”. Memory spikes and it is slower than expected. What is the better design?
o: A small pool of workers (about navigator.hardwareConcurrency - 1, capped) created once and fed from a queue
One worker per image, but created with type: 'classic'
Do the resizing on the main thread with requestIdleCallback
Use 60 service workers instead
qs.e: Each worker has its own JS engine instance, startup cost and memory. The CPU has only a few cores, so more workers than cores just compete. A fixed pool keeps parallelism without overhead. A page has at most one active service worker per scope, and they are not for CPU work.

qs.s: Offline users see the browser's own “No internet” page instead of your offline page. Read the service worker. What is wrong?

code.title: sw.js

o: Navigation requests cannot be intercepted by a service worker
fetch inside a service worker never rejects
/offline.html was never added to the cache, so caches.match resolves to undefined and respondWith fails with a network error. Precache it in install
respondWith must be called asynchronously
qs.e: The network-first logic is correct, but the fallback does not exist. caches.match does not throw on a miss; it returns undefined, which is not a valid response. Always precache fallback pages and test offline in DevTools.

interview.q: When would you use a Web Worker, when would you split work on the main thread, and when would you move work to the server?
answer: Worker: CPU-heavy work that needs no DOM and has data already on the client (parsing uploads, search index, image processing, diffing).
Main-thread chunking with scheduler.yield(): work that must touch the DOM or React state, or is too small to justify messaging.
Server: work that needs secrets or large data, is the same for many users (cacheable), or is too heavy for low-end phones.
Count the messaging cost: structured cloning large objects can cost more than the work; use transferables.
Measure INP and long tasks before and after; a worker that saves 20 ms is not worth the complexity.
followups: How would you cancel work in a worker when the user types a new query?
How does Comlink change the code, and what does it hide?

interview.q: Design the update strategy for a PWA's service worker so users never get stuck on a broken version.
answer: Serve sw.js with Cache-Control: no-cache so the browser always checks for a new version.
HTML network-first; hashed assets cache-first; versioned cache names; delete old caches only when no old client needs them.
When a new worker is waiting, show “New version, reload”; on click, postMessage it to call skipWaiting(), then reload on controllerchange.
Keep old hashed assets on the server for days so old tabs can still lazy-load chunks.
Prepare a kill switch: a worker at the same URL that unregisters itself and clears caches; know how to deploy it in minutes.
Monitor which SW version clients run (send it with error reports).
followups: Why is Clear-Site-Data sometimes used, and what does it remove?
What happens if sw.js itself is cached by a CDN for a day?

interview.q: How do you move data between the main thread and a worker efficiently?
answer: Default postMessage uses structured cloning: a deep copy, cost grows with size.
Transferables (ArrayBuffer, MessagePort, ImageBitmap, OffscreenCanvas, streams) move ownership with no copy; the sender can no longer use them.
SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics give real shared memory, but need cross-origin isolation (COOP + COEP) and careful synchronisation.
Send less: let the worker keep the big data and send back only results or diffs; batch small messages.
File/Blob are cheap to post; let the worker read and stream them itself.
followups: What happens to an ArrayBuffer in the sender after it is transferred?
How would you draw a chart in a worker?

one: Splitting one web app into independently built and deployed frontend pieces owned by different teams, composed at runtime or at the edge.
an: A shopping mall: one building and one entrance, but each shop is run and renovated independently.
how: Composition options: route-based (different paths are different apps behind one domain), Module Federation (load remote bundles at runtime), web components, or server-side/edge composition.
Shared concerns: design system, auth, routing, analytics. Version skew between pieces is the main hazard.
Like microservices, the main motive is team autonomy, not technology.
why: Large organisations with many frontend teams use them to stop stepping on each other in one deploy pipeline.
trade: Duplicate dependencies, inconsistent UX, harder performance budgets and complex local dev. For one or two teams, a well-structured monorepo is almost always better.

myth.m: Micro-frontends are the modern way to build any big app.
myth.r: They solve an organisational scaling problem and cost performance and consistency. Most teams do not have that problem.

q.s: A single 6-person frontend team proposes micro-frontends for their app. Most likely outcome?
o: Faster delivery
Overhead (versioning, duplication, tooling) without the team-autonomy payoff
Smaller bundles
Better SEO
q.e: The benefit is independent teams. One team gets only the costs.

more: Module Federation shared dependencies and version skew
Route-based composition with a shell app
lab: Follow the Module Federation quick start to load a remote component into a host app; then upgrade React in only one of them and see what breaks.

plain:
Micro-frontends split one web app into several smaller frontend apps, each owned and deployed by a different team, combined into what looks like one product.

Like microservices, the main goal is team independence. The cost is duplicated libraries, inconsistent UI risk, and harder performance control.
bridge: Imagine the header, the product catalogue and the checkout of a big shop built in three separate repos by three teams, each deploying whenever they want, loaded together in the browser.

walk.title: When it helps and when it hurts
steps: Big company: 8 frontend teams in one repo. Releases need everyone's sign-off; one team's bug blocks all.
They split by area: /catalog, /checkout, /account are separate apps behind one domain, sharing a design system.
Each team deploys independently, several times a day. Coordination drops.
Cost: React is loaded twice if versions differ; a shared component changes and two apps look different for a week.
Small team (one or two squads): the same split would add all the costs and none of the benefits.

terms: An independently deployed part of a frontend.
The app that loads and combines the parts.
A bundler feature for loading code from other deployed apps at runtime.
Different parts using different versions of a shared library.
insights: Most of the work is at the seams: shared dependencies, routing and the design system. Plan those before choosing a loading technology.
Each remote is a runtime dependency. When it is down or slow, the rest of the page must still work.
Independent deploys mean any two versions can meet in production, so contracts between pieces must stay backward compatible.

prod.summary: In production, micro-frontends trade one big deploy for many small ones, and the hard part moves to the seams: shared dependencies, version skew, design consistency, routing, and what happens when one remote is down. Seniors require a clear contract per piece, a single React instance, a performance budget for the whole page, and a fallback when a remote fails to load.
checklist: There is an organisational reason (several teams blocked by one release train), written down. Otherwise prefer a modular monorepo.
Route-based composition is the default; runtime composition (Module Federation) only where pieces must share one page.
React and the design system are shared as singletons with an agreed version range; CI fails if a remote needs an incompatible major.
Each remote is wrapped in an error boundary with a fallback UI, and remote loading has a timeout.
The total JS of a composed page has a budget; duplicate libraries are checked in the analyzer.
Cross-app communication goes through the URL or a small typed event contract, not shared global state.
Every remote can run locally against a deployed shell, so developers do not need to run all apps.
failures: “Invalid hook call. Hooks can only be called inside of the body of a function component.” only on pages that load the checkout remote.
Two copies of React are loaded (host and remote). Share react and react-dom as singleton with a compatible requiredVersion, and align versions.
The whole shell shows a white screen when the recommendations team's CDN has an outage.
The remote is imported without isolation. Load it lazily inside an error boundary with a fallback, so one piece failing does not break the page.
Buttons look slightly different between /catalog and /checkout for weeks.
Each app pins a different version of the design system. Publish the design system with semver, share it as a singleton, and track adoption of new versions.
Page weight grew to 2.5 MB of JS after the third micro-frontend joined.
Each app bundles its own copies of lodash, date libraries and polyfills. Agree on shared dependencies and a page-level budget enforced in CI.

code.title: Host config: shared singletons in Module Federation 2.0 (webpack)
code.note: singleton: true makes host and remotes use one copy of React; without it, hooks break across the boundary.

qs.s: Your company has 9 frontend teams in one Next.js app. Deploys happen once a week because every team must sign off. Which first step gives most of the autonomy with the least runtime risk?
o: Rewrite everything with Module Federation so each component is remote
Move to web components for all UI
Split by route: each area (/catalog, /checkout) becomes its own app behind one domain, sharing a design system package
Give each team its own subdomain with its own design
qs.e: Route-based splitting gives independent deploys with almost no runtime coupling. Fine-grained runtime federation adds version-skew and loading risks; separate designs break the product experience.

qs.s: The host uses React 19 and the new search remote was built with React 18. Both list react as shared with singleton: true. What is the likely result?
o: Both versions load and work independently
The build fails
Search gets its own React automatically
Only one React loads (the highest version); the remote runs against a major it was not built for, and you get a version warning and possible runtime bugs
qs.e: Singleton means one copy for everyone, so a major version mismatch becomes a runtime risk, not a build error. Align majors through a shared version policy checked in CI.

qs.s: A remote widget fails to load in 2% of sessions because of a regional CDN problem. Today that causes a blank page. What should the shell do?
o: Retry forever until it loads
Render the remote inside an error boundary with a timeout and a fallback, and report the failure to monitoring
Bundle every remote into the shell at build time
Show a browser alert
qs.e: Runtime composition must expect partial failure, like a service call. Isolating the failure keeps the rest of the page usable. Bundling everything at build time removes the independent deploys you wanted.

qs.s: Next.js multi-zones: the main app rewrites /checkout to the checkout app. Checkout pages load as HTML but without styles or JS (404 on /_next/static/...). What is the fix?

code.title: main app: next.config.ts

o: Give the checkout zone its own assetPrefix (e.g. /checkout-static) and add a rewrite for /checkout-static/:path+ to the checkout app
Copy the checkout app's .next/static folder into the main app at build time
Change the rewrites to redirects
Use Module Federation for the static files
qs.e: Both apps serve assets under /_next/static, so the browser asks the main app for files that only the checkout app has. A unique assetPrefix per zone plus a rewrite for it fixes the collision. Copying build output couples the deploys you wanted to separate; redirects would change the domain/URL the user sees.

qs.s: In the same multi-zone setup, the catalog app links to checkout with <Link href="/checkout">. Clicking it sometimes shows the catalog's 404 page. What is the right way to link between zones?
o: Add prefetch={false} to the Link
Wrap the Link in an error boundary
Use a plain <a href="/checkout"> so the browser does a full page load, which the rewrite sends to the checkout zone
Move /checkout into the catalog app's app folder as an empty page
qs.e: Link does a soft navigation inside the current app's router, which does not know the routes of another zone. Cross-zone navigation must be a hard navigation. That is the price of zones: moving between them reloads the page, so draw zone borders where users rarely cross.

qs.s: A remote reads data from the shell like this. Which contract is better for independent teams?

code.title: checkout remote

o: Keep it, but add try/catch around every access
Share the whole shell store as a Module Federation singleton
Copy the shell's store code into each remote

A small, typed, versioned contract: the shell passes needed data as props or URL, and remotes emit events like cart:item-added (payload type in a shared package); nobody touches another app's internal state
qs.e: Reaching into internal state couples every remote to the shell's data shape, so a refactor in one repo breaks others at runtime, which is exactly the coordination micro-frontends were meant to remove. Sharing the store as a singleton makes the coupling official, not smaller.

qs.s: The shell wraps the checkout remote in an error boundary, but when the remote's CDN is down the whole app is a white screen. The shell has import Checkout from 'checkout/App'; at the top of a file. Why does the boundary not help?
o: Error boundaries do not work with Module Federation

A static import is resolved while modules load, before React renders anything, so the failure never reaches the boundary. Load the remote with lazy(() => import('checkout/App')) inside <Suspense> and the boundary
The boundary needs a key to reset
The CDN returned HTML instead of JS, which boundaries ignore
qs.e: Error boundaries only catch errors thrown while rendering. A failed static import breaks the module graph of the shell itself. With lazy, the failed load becomes a rejected promise thrown during render, which the boundary catches and replaces with the fallback.

interview.q: We have 12 frontend teams on one SPA. Would you introduce micro-frontends? How do you decide?
answer: Start from the pain: measure lead time, how often releases are blocked by other teams, and build/test times. If the pain is build speed, a monorepo with affected builds may be enough.
If teams need independent releases, split along business domains that users rarely cross (catalog, checkout, account), usually by route first.
Define the shared platform: shell, design system, auth, analytics, error monitoring, and a page-level performance budget.
Use runtime composition (Module Federation) only where several teams must share one page.
Plan migration with the strangler pattern: carve out one area, learn, then continue; keep a way back.
followups: How do you handle the shared header and navigation?
How do you test the composed app end to end when every piece deploys alone?

interview.q: How do you handle shared dependencies and version skew with Module Federation?
answer: Share framework-level packages (React, React DOM, router, design system) as singletons with explicit requiredVersion ranges.
Have a version policy: everyone on the same major of React; CI checks the remote's declared range against the shell's.
Watch runtime warnings for unsatisfied versions and treat them as release blockers.
Do not share everything: small utility libraries can be bundled per remote; sharing adds loading coordination.
Upgrade majors with a coordinated plan (shell supports both, remotes move, shell drops old).
followups: What happens at runtime if a remote needs React 18 and the shell provides React 19 as a singleton?
How do you share CSS without conflicts?

interview.q: How do you keep UX and performance consistent across independently deployed frontends?
answer: One design system with semver, consumed as a shared package; track which version each app uses and set a support window.
Shared shell for header, navigation and layout so the frame never differs.
A page-level performance budget enforced in each pipeline, and RUM split by micro-frontend so regressions have an owner.
Shared quality gates: accessibility checks, visual regression on key flows, and a common error-tracking and analytics setup.
Governance: a platform team that owns the shell and contracts, with clear SLAs for requests from feature teams.
followups: Who decides when all apps must upgrade the design system?
How do you attribute a slow page to one team?

one: Many apps and packages in one repository, with tooling that builds and tests only what a change affects.
an: One shared workshop for several products, with a smart foreman who only re-tests the machines you actually touched.
how: Workspaces (pnpm, npm, yarn) link local packages. Build systems (Turborepo, Nx, Bazel) model the dependency graph, cache task outputs, and run only affected tasks.
Typical layout: apps/web, apps/api, packages/ui, packages/config, packages/types.
Atomic changes across app and shared library in one PR; one version of each dependency.
why: Shared types between frontend and backend, one design system, consistent tooling, and refactors across packages in a single commit.
trade: Without caching and affected-only CI, builds get slow. Ownership and module boundaries must be explicit (CODEOWNERS, lint rules).

myth.r: A monorepo is a code-storage choice. It can hold many independently deployed services.

q.s: CI takes 40 minutes in a monorepo because every package is tested on every PR. Fix?
o: Split into 30 repos
Use affected-only task execution plus remote caching (Turborepo/Nx)
Remove tests
Bigger CI machines only
q.e: The graph tells you what a change can affect; caching skips repeated work.

more: Internal packages: compiled vs just-in-time TS
lab: Create a pnpm workspace with Turborepo: apps/web, apps/api, packages/types. Share a type between web and api.
Run turbo build twice and see the cache hit; change one package and run turbo run build test --affected to see only affected tasks rerun.

plain: A monorepo keeps several apps and shared packages in one Git repository: for example the web app, the API, and shared types and UI components. Tools understand how the packages depend on each other, so they only rebuild and test what a change affects.
bridge: If you have ever copied the same TypeScript types between a frontend repo and a backend repo, a monorepo with a shared packages/types removes that copying.

walk.title: One change across frontend and backend
steps: Layout: apps/web, apps/api, packages/types, packages/ui.
You add a phone field to the User type in packages/types.
TypeScript immediately shows errors in both the API (must return it) and the web form (should display it).
You fix both in the same pull request. One review, one merge, no version mismatch.
CI with Turborepo runs tasks only for the affected packages and reuses cached results for the rest.

terms: Package manager feature linking local packages (pnpm, npm, yarn).
Which builds and tests depend on which.
Shared cache of build results across machines.
insights: The cache is only as correct as its keys. A missing env var in the key gives you a fast, wrong build.
Track CI time and cache hit rate over time. A slowly falling hit rate is the first sign of a broken task graph.
Boundaries do not enforce themselves: without lint rules, apps start importing each other's internal files.

prod.summary: In production, a monorepo succeeds or fails on its build system: correct task graph, correct cache keys and affected-only CI. Seniors watch CI time and cache hit rate, make sure every input that changes a build (files, env vars) is part of the cache key, and enforce boundaries so packages do not import each other's internals.
checklist: CI runs only affected tasks (turbo run build test --affected or nx affected) and uses a remote cache shared by CI and developers.
Every env var that changes build output is listed in turbo.json env/globalEnv; otherwise the cache returns a build made with old values.
outputs are declared for cached tasks (e.g. dist/**, .next/** without .next/cache/**).
Internal dependencies use the workspace:* protocol, so apps always use the local version.
Package boundaries are enforced: imports only through a package's exports, plus lint rules (Nx module boundaries, ESLint import rules).
CODEOWNERS maps folders to teams, so shared packages get reviews from their owners.
One version of core dependencies (React, TypeScript) across the repo, with a tool like syncpack or pnpm catalogs to keep them aligned.
numbers: Turborepo's default envMode is strict: tasks only see env vars listed in env/globalEnv (plus framework-inferred ones like NEXT_PUBLIC_*).
Turborepo --affected selects packages changed on the current branch versus the base branch; by default it works at package level, not per file.
failures: Production app calls the staging API, although the deploy set API_URL to production.
API_URL is not in the build task's env list, so Turborepo restored a cached build made with the staging value. Add it to env so it is part of the hash.
CI takes 45 minutes because every package builds and tests on every PR.
No affected filtering and no remote cache. Enable --affected and remote caching; aim for a high cache hit rate on unchanged packages.
A small change in packages/utils breaks three apps in production.
Apps import internal files (@acme/utils/src/x) and the change was not tested against them. Expose a public API via exports, and make CI run dependents of changed packages (which --affected does).
Type errors appear only in CI, never locally.
Packages are built in the wrong order or use stale dist types. Declare dependsOn: ["^build"] so dependencies build first, or use just-in-time TS packages.

code.title: turbo.json with correct cache inputs and outputs
code.note: ^build means “build my dependencies first”. Anything listed in env becomes part of the cache key; forgetting one is the classic wrong-cache bug.

qs.s: Two apps in a monorepo show different button styles after a release. apps/web depends on "@acme/ui": "workspace:*", apps/admin on "@acme/ui": "^2.1.0" from npm. What is going on?
o: Admin uses a published version from the registry while web uses the local source; they drift. Use workspace:* in both
pnpm cached the CSS
Turborepo did not rebuild admin
The design tokens are wrong
qs.e: Mixing local and registry versions of an internal package defeats the main benefit of a monorepo (one version, atomic changes). The workspace protocol always links the local package.

qs.s: Turborepo shows “FULL TURBO” (everything from cache) for a build, but the deployed site has the old feature flag value. The flag is read from process.env.FEATURE_X during build. Why?
o: Remote cache is corrupted
FEATURE_X is not listed in the task's env, so changing it does not change the cache hash
Next.js ignores env vars at build
--affected skipped the app
qs.e: Turborepo hashes only declared inputs. An undeclared env var means the old output is a “valid” cache hit. In strict mode the task would not even see the variable; declaring it fixes both.

qs.s: A team argues: “A monorepo means we must deploy all apps together.” What is the best reply?
o: True, that is the trade-off
True unless you use git submodules
Only for Nx, not for Turborepo
False: the repo is about code storage; each app can have its own pipeline that deploys only when it, or a package it depends on, changes
qs.e: Monorepo is not monolith. Affected detection tells each pipeline whether its app changed, so apps deploy independently while still sharing code and types.

qs.s: CI shows “FULL TURBO” for the build, then the deploy step fails with Cannot find module '/repo/packages/sdk/dist/index.js'. What is wrong?

code.title: turbo.json

o: The remote cache was deleted
dependsOn should be ["build"] without the caret
No outputs are declared, so Turborepo cached only the logs; on a cache hit it replays the logs but restores no dist files
The deploy step runs before Turborepo finishes uploading
qs.e: Turborepo can only restore files it was told to cache. Without outputs (e.g. ["dist/**"]) a cache hit restores nothing on a fresh CI machine. Removing the caret would change the meaning to “build this package's own build first”, which is a cycle, not a fix.

qs.s: The repo moved from npm workspaces to pnpm. Now apps/web fails with “Module not found: Can't resolve 'lodash'”. Nobody changed web's code. Why?

code.title: apps/web/package.json

o: pnpm does not support lodash
apps/web imports lodash but never declared it (a phantom dependency). npm hoisted lodash to the root because @acme/utils uses it; pnpm's strict layout does not. Add lodash to web's dependencies
workspace:* must be replaced with a version number
The pnpm lockfile is corrupted; delete it
qs.e: Hoisting made undeclared imports work by accident. pnpm only links a package's declared dependencies into its node_modules, which surfaces these bugs. The fix is to declare what you import, not to turn hoisting back on.

qs.s: Your team considers “just-in-time” internal packages: packages/ui exports ./src/index.ts directly, with no build step. What is a real downside?
o: Every consuming app must compile the TypeScript itself (e.g. Next.js transpilePackages), and the package's compile work cannot be cached as its own Turborepo task
TypeScript cannot follow imports into other packages
Apps cannot hot-reload changes from the package
It cannot be used with pnpm workspaces
qs.e: JIT packages are simple and give instant hot reload, but they push compile and type-check work into every consumer and only work when every consumer uses a bundler that handles TS. Compiled packages cost a build step but are cacheable and can be published.

qs.s: The build fails after packages/ui added an exports field. What is the right fix?

code.title: build log
code.src:
apps/admin/src/Settings.tsx
  import { Button } from '@acme/ui/src/components/Button';

Error [ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED]: Package subpath './src/components/Button'
is not defined by "exports" in /repo/packages/ui/package.json

o: Remove the exports field so all files are reachable again
Add a TypeScript paths alias to the file
Copy Button into apps/admin
Import from the public entry (import { Button } from '@acme/ui'), or have the ui team add a deliberate subpath export if one is needed
qs.e: exports defines the package's public API; the error is the boundary working as intended. Deep imports into src let other teams depend on internals, so any refactor can break them. A paths alias would hide the problem from TypeScript only.

interview.q: How would you set up CI for a 40-package monorepo so PRs take under 10 minutes?
answer: Model the task graph correctly (dependsOn, outputs, env inputs) so caching is safe.
Run only affected tasks against the merge base, and use a remote cache shared by CI and developers.
Parallelise across machines or jobs for the remaining work, with the slowest tests split into shards.
Cache the package store (pnpm store) and avoid full reinstalls; use a frozen lockfile.
Watch cache hit rate and the slowest tasks weekly; a sudden drop in hit rate usually means an undeclared or noisy input (timestamps, env vars).
Run a full build on main nightly as a safety net for graph mistakes.
followups: How do you prove a cache hit is safe?
What makes a task non-deterministic and how do you find it?

interview.q: How do you enforce boundaries and ownership in a monorepo?
answer: Each package exposes a public API through exports; deep imports fail.
Lint rules for allowed dependencies between layers or domains (Nx module boundaries with tags, ESLint import rules, dependency-cruiser).
CODEOWNERS per folder so changes to shared packages need the owning team's review.
Every package declares its dependencies (pnpm's strict layout catches phantom ones).
Keep shared packages small and purposeful; a growing utils package is a smell.
followups: How would you stop the web app from importing server-only code from apps/api?
How do you handle a shared package owned by nobody?

interview.q: Monorepo or polyrepo for a company with web, mobile and API teams? How do you decide?
answer: Monorepo wins when code is shared and changes cross boundaries often: shared types/contracts, a design system, atomic refactors.
Polyrepo wins when teams are independent, use different toolchains, or need strict access control per repo.
The monorepo cost is tooling: task graph, remote cache, affected CI, ownership rules; without them it gets slow and tangled.
Polyrepo cost is coordination: publishing versions, upgrading consumers, contract drift between client and API.
A middle path is common: one repo for the web+API+shared packages, mobile separate if its toolchain differs a lot.
followups: How do you share API types with a mobile app in another repo?
What would make you split a monorepo?

one: A shared set of design tokens, components, patterns and guidelines that keeps a product consistent and fast to build.
an: LEGO: a fixed set of well-made bricks everyone builds with, instead of each team carving their own.
how: Layers: tokens (colour, spacing, type, radius as variables) → primitives (accessible button, input, dialog; often headless libraries like Radix or React Aria) → components → patterns (forms, empty states).
Documented in Storybook or a docs site; visual regression tests catch unintended changes.
Theming (dark mode, brands) works through tokens, not per-component overrides.
why: Consistency, accessibility built in once, faster feature work, and a shared language between design and engineering.
trade: A design system is a product with users; without ownership it rots. Over-abstracted components with 40 props are worse than a little duplication.

myth.m: Installing a component library is a design system.
myth.r: A library is parts. A system includes tokens, rules, docs and governance for your product.

q.s: Teams keep forking the shared Button because it lacks variants they need. Root issue?
o: Too few colours
The design system lacks an ownership/contribution process to evolve with product needs
React version
CSS-in-JS
q.e: Systems need a way for consumers to request and contribute changes, or forks multiply.

lab: Define colour, spacing and type tokens as CSS variables with a dark theme. Build Button, Input and Dialog on Radix primitives using only tokens. Document them in Storybook.

plain:
A design system is a shared set of building blocks for a product's UI: design tokens (colours, spacing, typography as variables), accessible components (buttons, inputs, dialogs), patterns (forms, empty states), and documentation on how to use them.

It makes the product consistent and makes building new screens much faster.
bridge: shadcn/ui, Material UI and Chakra are component libraries. A design system is your product's own version: built on such libraries or primitives, but with your tokens, rules and docs.

walk.title: Changing the brand colour in one place
steps: Tokens: --color-accent, --space-2, --radius-md, defined once with light and dark values.
Components (Button, Input, Badge) use only tokens, never hard-coded colours.
Marketing asks to change the brand colour.
You change --color-accent in one file. Every button, link and badge in every app updates, in both themes.
Without tokens, someone would search and replace hex codes in 200 files and miss some.

terms: A named design value, like a colour or spacing, stored as a variable.
A low-level accessible building block (Radix, React Aria).
A tool to develop and document components in isolation.
Comparing screenshots to catch unintended UI changes.
insights: Count local copies of components in product repos: each copy is a request the design system did not answer.
A change to a shared component reaches every app at once. Screenshot (visual regression) tests are the only safe way to review it.
Adoption depends on developer experience: clear docs, copy-paste examples and fast answers matter more than the number of components.

prod.summary: In production, a design system is a product with versions, users and support. Seniors care that tokens drive theming, base components are accessible once, changes are released with semver and changelogs, and visual regressions are caught before they reach every app. Adoption and the number of local forks tell you if it is working.
checklist: Two token layers: primitive (blue-600) and semantic (color-accent, color-danger-bg); components use only semantic tokens.
Dark mode and brands are new token values, not new component code.
Base components pass keyboard and screen reader checks and meet contrast (4.5:1 text, 3:1 UI borders and icons).
Every component has Storybook stories for its states (hover, focus, disabled, error, long text, RTL) and runs visual regression tests in CI.
Releases follow semver; breaking changes come with a codemod or migration notes.
There is a public contribution process (issue template, office hours, response time), so teams request variants instead of forking.
Usage is measured: which components and versions each app uses, and how many local copies exist.
numbers: The W3C Design Tokens Community Group published the first stable Design Tokens Format (2025.10) on 28 October 2025; files use $value/$type and .tokens.json.
WCAG 2.2 contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and for UI components/graphics (SC 1.4.3 and 1.4.11).
failures: Dark mode has unreadable grey-on-grey text in three places.
Those components used primitive tokens or hard-coded hex values, so the theme switch missed them. Use only semantic tokens, and add a lint rule that bans raw colours.
A small Button padding change broke layouts in 40 screens across 5 apps.
The change shipped as a patch with no visual tests. Run visual regression (Chromatic or Playwright screenshots) on stories and release layout-affecting changes as minor with notes.
Teams have 6 different copies of “Modal”.
The system lacks a needed variant and has no contribution path. Add composition slots (header/footer/children) instead of more props, and offer a fast request process.
The shared Dialog fails an accessibility audit in every app at once.
Focus trapping and labelling were custom-built. Build on proven primitives (native <dialog>, Radix, React Aria) and test with keyboard and a screen reader in CI stories.

code.title: Primitive and semantic tokens in the DTCG format
code.note: accent is an alias of a primitive. A rebrand or dark theme changes what the alias points to; components never change. Tools like Style Dictionary turn this file into CSS variables, iOS and Android values.

qs.s: Marketing wants a second brand (different colours and radius) for a partner site using the same components. With a good token setup, what is the main work?
o: Fork the component library
Add a brand prop to every component
Rewrite styles with a new CSS framework
Provide a new set of semantic token values for the partner brand and load them on that site
qs.e: When components only read semantic tokens, a brand is a new token set. A brand prop on every component spreads theming logic everywhere; a fork doubles maintenance.

qs.s: Your Button has 38 props (iconLeft, iconRight, badge, tooltip, ...). New requests keep coming. What is the better direction?
o: Add the props; it keeps one component
Composition: a small Button that accepts children and slots, plus a few documented patterns built from it
Let each team fork Button
Generate props from Figma automatically
qs.e: Configuration explodes because every combination needs a prop. Composition lets teams build variants from stable parts without changing the core.

qs.s: A token change makes color-text-muted lighter. CI is green, but users report hard-to-read labels. What check was missing?
o: Unit tests for the token file
A bigger Storybook
An automated contrast check of semantic token pairs (text on background) against WCAG 4.5:1, plus visual regression
TypeScript strict mode
qs.e: Token changes affect every screen. Checking text/background pairs for contrast catches this class of bug before release; unit tests on JSON do not know about readability.

qs.s: The design system ships its CSS inside a cascade layer. An app adds its own override. Which background does the button get?

code.title: styles

o: The accent colour, because the design system selector has higher specificity
Red, because unlayered styles beat any layered styles, whatever the specificity
The accent colour, because the layer was declared first
It depends on which file the browser downloads first
qs.e: Cascade layers are compared before specificity, and normal unlayered styles win over all layers. That is why design systems put their CSS in a layer: apps can override with simple selectors without specificity wars. (For !important rules the order is reversed.)

qs.s: Review this usage. What is the problem, and what does a good design system offer for it?

code.title: SettingsLink.tsx
code.src:
<Button
  variant="ghost"
  onClick={() => router.push('/settings')}
>
  Settings
</Button>

o: Nothing; buttons and links are the same for screen readers
router.push is slower than a link
The variant should be link instead of ghost

It is navigation built as a button: no “open in new tab”, no link semantics for screen readers, no prefetch. The system should let the Button style render a real link, e.g. <Button asChild><Link href="/settings">
qs.e: Navigation should be an <a>; actions should be a <button>. Patterns like asChild (Radix Slot) or a render prop keep the look while rendering the correct element. A link variant only changes the style, not the element.

qs.s: The token color-text-subtle must be renamed to color-text-muted. 30 apps use it. What is the safest release plan?
o: Add the new name, keep the old one as a deprecated alias with a lint warning, ship a codemod, then remove the alias in the next major after usage reaches zero
Rename it in a patch release; apps will see the change on their next install
Keep both names forever
Ask every team to update by Friday, then rename
qs.e: A rename is a breaking change for consumers. Aliases make the change non-breaking for now, the codemod makes migration cheap, usage tracking tells you when removal is safe, and semver signals the final break. Keeping both forever makes the token set confusing.

qs.s: The shared Popover looks perfect in Storybook. Inside a product card it is cut off at the card's edge, although it uses position: fixed. What is the cause and fix?

code.title: card.css

o: position: fixed is not supported inside flex containers
The popover's z-index is too low; set it to 9999

transform on an ancestor makes it the containing block for fixed elements, so the popover is positioned and clipped inside the card. Render it in a portal to body, or use the browser top layer (popover API, <dialog>)
Storybook uses a different CSS reset
qs.e: Any transform, filter or contain on an ancestor changes what fixed is relative to, and overflow: hidden then clips it. No z-index can escape that. Portals or the top layer take the element out of the card's box entirely.

interview.q: How would you build a design system that serves 5 product teams and 2 brands?
answer: Tokens first: primitive and semantic layers, a theme per brand and mode, stored in one source (DTCG format) and generated to CSS variables and native platforms.
Build components on accessible headless primitives (React Aria, Radix, native elements) and only read semantic tokens.
Ship as a versioned package with semver, changelogs, Storybook docs and visual regression and a11y checks in CI.
A small core team owns it, with a contribution model (RFCs, office hours) so teams extend it instead of forking.
Measure adoption: component usage per app, versions in use, number of local overrides.
followups: How do you handle a brand that wants a different border radius and font?
What do you do when a team needs a component tomorrow and the system cannot deliver it?

interview.q: How do you roll out a breaking change in a design system used by 30 apps?
answer: Avoid breaking where possible: add new APIs next to old ones and deprecate with console/lint warnings.
Provide a codemod and migration notes; test the codemod on real consumer repos.
Release as a major; support the previous major for a fixed window with security and critical fixes.
Track usage of the deprecated API across repos to know when it is safe to remove.
Coordinate with visual regression tests in consumer apps for layout-affecting changes.
followups: How do you find every usage of a component prop across 30 repos?
Would you ever ship two major versions in one app at the same time?

interview.q: Headless primitives, a styled component library, or copy-in components (shadcn/ui): what are the trade-offs?
answer: Styled library (MUI, Chakra): fastest start, but your brand fights its styles and upgrades can be large.
Headless primitives (React Aria, Radix): the hard behaviour (focus, keyboard, ARIA) is solved; you own all styling; best base for a custom system.
Copy-in (shadcn/ui): you own the code, easy to change; but each copy drifts and upstream fixes do not reach you automatically.
For a company system, a common choice is headless primitives inside your own versioned package, possibly starting from copied shadcn code.
Decide by brand needs, team size and who will maintain accessibility.
followups: How do you get upstream bug fixes into copied components?
What accessibility work is still yours when using headless primitives?

Design tokens explained.

one: Building interfaces usable by people with visual, motor, hearing and cognitive differences, guided by WCAG.
an: Ramps and lifts in a building. Designed for wheelchair users, used gladly by everyone with a pram or suitcase.
how: Semantic HTML first: button, a, label, headings, landmarks. ARIA only fills gaps; wrong ARIA is worse than none.
Keyboard: everything reachable and operable, visible focus, logical order, focus management in dialogs.

Contrast (WCAG AA: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI parts), text alternatives for images, not relying on colour alone, targets at least 24×24 CSS px (WCAG 2.2), respecting prefers-reduced-motion.

Test with a screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA), keyboard only, and automated checks (axe). Automated tools find many issues by count (Deque reports about 57%), but many WCAG criteria (meaningful alt text, focus order, clear errors) need a human.
why: Legal requirements in many markets (European Accessibility Act from 2025, ADA), larger audience, better SEO and usability for everyone.
trade: Retrofitting is expensive; building it into the design system makes it nearly free.

myth.m: Adding aria-labels everywhere makes a site accessible.
myth.r: A clickable div with an aria-label is still not focusable or keyboard-operable. Use a real button.

q.s: A custom dropdown is a div with onClick. Keyboard users cannot open it. Simplest robust fix?
o: Add aria-label
Use a native select, or an accessible primitive (Radix/React Aria) that handles keyboard and ARIA
Add tabindex=1
Add a tooltip
q.e: Native elements and proven primitives bring correct keyboard and screen reader behaviour.

more: Focus traps and returning focus after dialogs
lab: Navigate one of your apps with keyboard only (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Esc). Write down every place you got stuck.
Turn on VoiceOver (Cmd+F5 on macOS) and complete one task with your eyes closed.
Run axe DevTools and fix the top three issues.

plain:
Accessibility means everyone can use your interface: people who are blind (screen readers), who cannot use a mouse (keyboard only), who have low vision (contrast, zoom), or cognitive differences. WCAG is the standard checklist.

Most of it comes for free from using the right HTML elements.
bridge: A <div onClick> works with a mouse but cannot be reached with Tab, does not respond to Enter, and is not announced as a button by screen readers. A <button> does all of that automatically.

walk.title: Testing a sign-up form without a mouse
steps: Press Tab from the top of the page. Can you see where focus is at every step? (Visible focus styles.)
Reach each input. Does the screen reader announce its label? (A real <label for>, not just placeholder text.)
Submit with errors. Is the error announced and linked to its field? (aria-describedby, focus moves to the first error.)
Open the terms dialog. Is focus trapped inside, and does Escape close it and return focus to the link?
Run axe DevTools for the automatic checks. It finds the common, countable issues (contrast, missing labels); the manual steps above find the rest.

terms: Software that reads the page aloud (VoiceOver, NVDA).
Attributes that add accessibility information when HTML alone is not enough.
Controlling where keyboard focus goes, especially in dialogs.
Text vs background brightness difference; 4.5:1 for normal text.
insights: Automated checks catch the countable problems. Only a keyboard and screen reader pass tells you whether a person can finish the task.
Treat an a11y bug in checkout like any other bug that blocks payment: real users cannot buy.
Most fixes are cheap at design time (labels, focus order, contrast) and expensive after release.

prod.summary: In production, accessibility is a legal and quality requirement that you protect with process: accessible primitives in the design system, automated checks in CI, and regular manual keyboard and screen reader passes on key flows. Seniors focus on the flows that make money or matter most (sign-up, checkout, forms) and treat a11y regressions like functional bugs.
checklist: Core flows (sign-up, login, checkout, main form) can be completed with keyboard only and with a screen reader.
axe (e.g. @axe-core/playwright) runs in CI on key pages and fails the build on serious/critical violations.
Every input has a visible <label>; errors are linked with aria-describedby and announced.
Focus is visible everywhere (:focus-visible styles), never removed with outline: none without a replacement.
Dialogs trap focus, close on Escape and return focus to the opener (native <dialog> with showModal() does this).
The page has lang, one h1, a logical heading order and landmarks (header, nav, main).
Animations respect prefers-reduced-motion; nothing flashes more than 3 times per second.
numbers: WebAIM Million 2026: 95.9% of the top 1,000,000 home pages had detectable WCAG 2 failures; 83.9% had low-contrast text.
WCAG contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (24 px, or 18.66 px bold) and for UI components.
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (AA): pointer targets at least 24×24 CSS pixels, or enough spacing.
The European Accessibility Act has applied to many consumer products and services, including e-commerce, since 28 June 2025.
failures: Screen reader users say “the form just says ‘edit text’ for every field”.
Inputs use placeholder instead of labels. Add a <label for> (it can be visually styled small), and connect help/error text with aria-describedby.
Keyboard users get stuck behind an open modal; Tab goes to the page underneath.
A custom div modal without focus management. Use <dialog> with showModal() (makes the rest inert) or a tested primitive like Radix/React Aria.
axe passes, but a blind tester cannot complete checkout.

Automated tools cannot judge order, meaning or flow: a “Continue” button is an unlabeled icon, and the total updates silently. Add accessible names, an aria-live region for the total, and manual testing per release.
Customer complaint: “I zoomed to 200% and the Pay button disappeared.”
Fixed heights and overflow: hidden clip content. Use flexible layouts and test at 200% zoom and 320 px width (WCAG reflow).

code.title: An accessible confirm dialog with the native dialog element
code.note: form method="dialog" closes the dialog without JS and sets returnValue. showModal() moves focus to the first focusable element, so the safe action (Cancel) comes first. Do not rely on React's autoFocus here: on a client render React only calls focus() at mount, while the dialog is still closed, and does not write the autofocus attribute the dialog looks for.

qs.s: An icon-only button <button><svg .../></button> closes a panel. axe reports “Buttons must have discernible text”. Best fix?
o: Add title="x" to the SVG
Add aria-label="Close panel" to the button (or visually hidden text) and aria-hidden="true" on the SVG
Replace the button with a div role="button"
Add tabindex="0"
qs.e: The button is already focusable and operable; it only lacks an accessible name. A div with a role would lose built-in keyboard behaviour. Hiding the decorative SVG avoids double announcements.

qs.s: Your designer picks grey #999 text on white for helper text. The contrast ratio is about 2.8:1. Is this acceptable for WCAG AA body-size text?
o: No: normal-size text needs at least 4.5:1
Yes: helper text is exempt
Yes, if the font is bold
Yes: 3:1 is the rule for all text
qs.e: 4.5:1 applies to normal text; 3:1 applies only to large text (24 px, or about 18.66 px bold) and UI components. Helper text carries information, so it is not exempt.

qs.s: A search page updates the result count (“24 results”) without reloading. Sighted users notice; screen reader users do not. What fixes this with the least noise?
o: Move focus to the result count on every keystroke
Use alert()
Put the count in a polite live region (role="status") and update its text after the results settle
Add aria-label to the input
qs.e: A polite live region announces changes without stealing focus. Moving focus on every keystroke interrupts typing, and alerts are disruptive. Debounce the update so it is not announced for every letter.

qs.s: When a modal opens, the code sets aria-hidden="true" on <main>. Keyboard users report that Tab moves to buttons behind the modal, and the screen reader says nothing there. Why?

code.title: Layout.tsx
code.src:
<main aria-hidden={modalOpen}>
  <ProductList />   {/* contains buttons and links */}
</main>
{modalOpen && <CustomModal onClose={close} />}

o: aria-hidden needs the value "hidden", not "true"
Screen readers ignore aria-hidden on landmarks
aria-hidden only hides content from assistive tech; it does not stop focus. Use the inert attribute on <main> (or native <dialog> with showModal(), which makes the rest inert)
The modal must be rendered before <main> in the DOM
qs.e: Focusable elements inside aria-hidden are a known failure: focus lands on something the screen reader cannot describe. inert removes the subtree from both focus order and the accessibility tree. In React 19, inert is a normal boolean prop.

qs.s: A screen reader user hears “Email, edit text, invalid entry” but never hears what is wrong. Which fix?

code.title: signup.html
code.src: Enter an address like name@example.com

o: Give the error an id and add aria-describedby="email-error" to the input, so the message is read with the field; also move focus to the first invalid field on submit
Make the error text red and bold
Add role="alert" to every error that is always in the page
Put the error text in the input's placeholder
qs.e: aria-invalid says that something is wrong, not what. aria-describedby links the message to the field. Colour alone fails WCAG 1.4.1. Permanent role="alert" elements are not announced reliably and can be noisy; placeholders disappear when typing.

qs.s: In a Vite + React Router app, a user clicks “Orders” in the side menu. The content changes, but a screen reader user hears nothing and focus stays on the menu link. What is the standard fix?
o: Add aria-live="assertive" to the whole <main>
Reload the full page on every navigation
Add tabindex="0" to every heading
After navigation, update document.title and move focus to the new page's <h1> (with tabindex="-1"), or announce the page title in a polite live region
qs.e: Client-side routing skips the browser's normal page-load announcement. Moving focus to the heading tells the user where they are and starts reading from the right place. A live <main> would read the whole page on every change; tabindex="0" on headings adds useless Tab stops. (Next.js has a built-in route announcer for this.)

qs.s: After saving, this toast appears visually, but screen readers often say nothing. Why?

code.title: SaveStatus.tsx

o: role="status" is only for errors
The live region is inserted together with its text; many screen readers only announce changes inside a region that already existed. Render an empty role="status" element always and change its text
The text is too short to be announced
React removes ARIA roles from conditionally rendered elements
qs.e: Screen readers register live regions when they appear in the accessibility tree and then watch them for changes. Adding the region and the message at the same moment is often missed. Keep the container mounted (it can be visually hidden) and update its content.

interview.q: How do you make accessibility part of the process in a team that ships every week?
answer: Build it into the design system: accessible primitives, focus styles, contrast-checked tokens, so most screens get it for free.
Automate the countable part: eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y in the editor, axe in component tests and Playwright on key pages, failing CI on serious violations.
Add acceptance criteria to stories (keyboard path, labels, announcements) and check them in review.
Do a manual keyboard and screen reader pass on critical flows each release; run an expert audit periodically.
Track a11y bugs like other bugs, with severity, and include people with disabilities in user testing where possible.
followups: Which screen reader and browser combinations do you test, and why?
How do you handle a legal deadline like the European Accessibility Act?

interview.q: Walk me through building an accessible autocomplete (combobox).
answer: Follow the WAI-ARIA APG combobox pattern: an input with role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-controls pointing at a role="listbox" of role="option" items.
Keep DOM focus in the input and point at the highlighted option with aria-activedescendant; mark it with aria-selected.
Keyboard: Down/Up move, Enter selects, Escape closes (and clears on a second press), Tab leaves without trapping.
Announce the number of results in a polite live region, debounced; handle loading and empty states.
Test with VoiceOver and NVDA, because support differs. In practice, prefer a proven implementation (React Aria, Downshift) over building it yourself.
followups: Why aria-activedescendant instead of moving real focus to options?
How do you handle results that load asynchronously?

interview.q: What can automated accessibility testing catch, what can it not, and how do you cover the rest?
answer: It catches rule-based issues: missing labels and alt attributes, contrast, invalid ARIA, duplicate IDs, missing lang. Deque's data says about 57% of issues by count.
It cannot judge meaning or experience: whether alt text is useful, focus order is logical, error messages are clear, a custom widget is operable, or announcements happen at the right time.
Cover the rest with keyboard-only and screen reader walkthroughs of key flows, zoom/reflow checks at 200% and 320 px, and reduced-motion checks.
Write tests for behaviour you fixed (focus returns after a dialog, live region updates) with Testing Library queries by role and name.
Periodic expert audits and feedback from real users close the gap.
followups: Why do queries like getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }) improve accessibility?

diagrams.caption: What to notice: assistive technology reads the accessibility tree, built from your HTML. A <button> gives role, focus and Enter/Space for free; a <div> gives none of them.

diagrams.title: Focus management in a modal dialog
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as Keyboard user
  participant L as Terms link
  participant D as dialog (showModal)
  U->>L: Enter
  L->>D: open
  Note over D: focus moves inside, page behind is inert
  U->>D: Tab, Tab
  Note over D: focus stays inside the dialog
  U->>D: Escape
  D-->>L: close, focus returns to link
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the user never loses their place. Native <dialog> with showModal() gives you the inert background and Escape; check that focus returns to the opener.

codeCheck.detail: In Chrome: showModal() focused Cancel, the dialog had the right accessible name and description, the page behind was not focusable, Esc closed it and focus returned to the opener, Delete set returnValue “delete” and called onConfirm once.
